docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Flutter] Mobile Framework

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course shows, step by step, how to write a mobile application with the Flutter framework and the Dart language: an Android application whose screens are built on the phone from the JSON data of a server. The same code also produces a web application.

After setting up the working environment, it relies on 25 small examples, each focused on a single concept: StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget, setState, the widget tree, input fields, validation with Form and FormField; widget composition, the widget life cycle, InheritedWidget, animations; routing with go_router and its guards; asynchronous code and shared state (Future, Stream, FutureBuilder, provider, shared_preferences); internationalization; and finally talking to the server.

The server is treated as a black box: it is the JSON server of the RdvMedecins application, written with NestJS. You install it, study its API and query it with 48 curl examples, without having to read its code.

Then comes a complete case study: the Flutter client of RdvMedecins, an appointment-booking application for a medical practice, in which every file is commented, followed by its deployment.

Prerequisites: the basics of the Dart language, presented in the course Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples. The 25 examples have the same numbers as those of the React course; the same screens are also written with Vue.js and Angular.

All courses by Serge Tahé

docs.title: 14.1. Installing Flutter
docs.text:
The [Flutter] SDK can be downloaded from docs.flutter.dev (select [Windows], then [Android]). It is a simple compressed folder, which you extract into a folder WITHOUT spaces or accented characters (e.g., [C:\dev\flutter]), then add its subfolder [bin] to the user’s environment variable [Path]. The [Dart] SDK is included. Verify the installation in a new console:

flutter --version
flutter doctor

[flutter doctor] checks everything that [Flutter] requires: SDK, [Android], and its licenses, [Chrome], [Visual Studio] (for [Windows] applications), connected devices, and network access. Each line is preceded by a checkmark [√] if everything is okay, an X [X] or an exclamation point [!] otherwise, with instructions on what to do listed below. [flutter doctor -v] provides details (versions, paths).

The “Visual Studio” line applies only to [Windows] applications (the [windows/] examples folder): it may remain in error if you’re targeting only mobile and web.

In [Windows], projects that use native code packages ([shared_preferences]...) require the system’s “developer mode”: [flutter pub get] indicates this (“Building with plugins requires symlink support”). You can enable it in Settings / System / For developers (command [start ms-settings:developers]).

docs.title: 14.2. Installing Android Studio and an emulator
docs.text:
[Android Studio] can be downloaded from developer.android.com/studio. It is not used to write code, but to install the [Android] SDK and create an emulator:

  • Upon first launch, the wizard installs the [Android] SDK;
  • More Actions menu / SDK Manager, SDK Tools tab: check “Android SDK Command-line Tools,” which [Flutter] requires;
  • in a console: [flutter doctor --android-licenses], and accept the licenses;
  • More Actions / Virtual Device Manager menu: create a virtual phone (for example, a “Pixel”) using a recent system image. Click the ▶ button to launch it; [flutter devices] will then detect it under the name [emulator-5554]. You can also launch it without opening [Android Studio]: [flutter emulators] lists the emulators, and [flutter emulators --launch <name>] launches one.

For a real phone: In Settings / About Phone, tapping “Build Number” seven times brings up “Developer Options,” where you can enable “USB Debugging.” When connected to the computer, the phone will ask you to authorize the computer; [flutter devices] will then detect it.

docs.title: 14.3. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is downloaded from code.visualstudio.com. In the Extensions panel (Ctrl-Shift-X), install the [Flutter] extension (from [Dart Code]), which also installs the [Dart] extension. They provide:

  • code completion, code validation as you type (using the rules from [analysis_options.yaml]), navigation to the definition of a widget or class, and renaming across the entire project;
  • code formatting upon saving ([dart format]);
  • device selection, in the lower-right corner of the window (or the “Flutter: Select Device” command);
  • launching via F5 (debugging: breakpoints, variables); each time a file is saved, the app is reloaded on the fly;
  • actions on widgets (Ctrl-. on a widget): “Wrap with Padding,” “Wrap with Column,” “Extract Widget,” etc.—very useful for reorganizing a widget tree.

To run an example using F5, open its file [main.dart] before pressing F5 (or create a file named [.vscode/launch.json]). Open a project via the File / Open Folder menu (the [examples_flutter] folder, for example), and open a console via the Terminal / New Terminal menu.

docs.title: 14.4. The Flutter tool DevTools
docs.text:
[Flutter DevTools] is included with the SDK. While the application is running, [flutter run] displays its address (“The Flutter DevTools debugger and profiler... is available at: http://127.0.0.1:9101... ”); in [VS Code], the “Flutter: Open DevTools” command opens it in the editor. Its most useful tabs:

  • “Flutter Inspector”: the widget tree for the screen, and the properties for each widget. “Select Widget Mode” lets you tap an element on the phone to find its widget in the tree; “Show Guidelines” draws the margins and alignment lines. This is the tool that answers the question, “Why isn’t this widget in the right place?”;
  • “Performance” and “CPU Profiler”: the time spent rendering and drawing each frame, to identify the cause of a choppy animation;
  • “Network”: the application’s HTTP requests, including their headers and bodies; here you can see the token cookie being sent and returned;
  • “Logging”: what the application displays ([debugPrint]).

docs.title: 14.5. Installation of Node.js
docs.text:
[Node.js] is downloaded from nodejs.org: select version LTS (long-term support). The [Windows] installer also installs [npm]. It is only required for the JSON server. Verify the installation in a console:

node --version
npm --version

docs.title: 14.6. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
The JSON server requires [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]). [Laragon] (laragon.org) installs one under [Windows], ready to use, with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the “Start All” button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values from the server’s [.env.example] file;
  • in [HeidiSQL] (the “Database” button), the File / Run SQL File menu item runs the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script.

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and run the script using the command-line client: [mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql].

docs.title: 14.7. Installing curl
docs.text:
[curl] is included with [Windows] versions 10 and 11, [macOS], and most distributions of [Linux]. Check its version:

curl --version

The option [--json], used in this document, has been available since version 7.82 (2022). If you are using an older version, replace [--json @file] with [-H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @file], or install a recent version from curl.se.

In [PowerShell], you must enter [curl.exe], not [curl]: In [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which does not include the options from [curl]. The command prompt ([cmd]) does not have this issue.

docs.title: 6.1. Example 19: Future, Stream, and Timers
docs.text:
Many things happen “later”: timer ticks, keystrokes, a server’s response. [Dart] has two types for this, at the core of the language:

  • [Future<T>]: ONE value, later (a server’s response, a choice made in a window);
  • [Stream<T>]: a SEQUENCE of values over time (ticks, messages, GPS positions...).

[Flutter] has a widget to display each one, rebuilding it when a value arrives: [FutureBuilder] and [StreamBuilder]. And for what must happen after a delay: [Timer].

// =========================================================================
// lib/ex19_asynchronous/main.dart - Future, Stream, timers
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Many things happen "later": the ticks of a timer, the
// keystrokes, the response of a server. Dart has two types for
// this, at the heart of the language:
//   - Future<T>: ONE value, later (the response of a server);
//   - Stream<T>: a SEQUENCE of values, over time (ticks,
//     messages...).
// Flutter has a widget to display each one, rebuilding it when a
// value arrives: FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder.
// And for what must happen after a delay: Timer (dart:async).
// =========================================================================

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:math';

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

const doctors = ['Marie PELISSIER', 'Paul TATOU', 'Sophie DUPONT', 'Jacques DURAND', 'Martine PELLETIER'];
final _random = Random();

// a simulated "server": the response (a Future) arrives after a random delay
Future<List<String>> search(String text) async {
  await Future<void>.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 200 + _random.nextInt(600)));
  return doctors.where((m) => m.toLowerCase().contains(text)).toList();
}

// 1. a Stream produced by an "async*" function: each yield SENDS a
// value to those who listen to the Stream
Stream<int> countdown(int start) async* {
  for (var remaining = start; remaining >= 0; remaining--) {
    yield remaining;
    if (remaining > 0) await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
  }
}

String currentTime() => DateTime.now().toString().substring(11, 19);

void main() {
  runApp(
    MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      home: const AsynchronousPage(),
    ),
  );
}

class AsynchronousPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const AsynchronousPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<AsynchronousPage> createState() => _AsynchronousPageState();
}

class _AsynchronousPageState extends State<AsynchronousPage> {
  final List<String> _log = [];
  // the Stream and the Future are created ONCE (and not on each build:
  // each call of build would restart the countdown!)
  final Stream<int> _countdown = countdown(20);
  // 3. a Future that completes after one second
  final Future<String> _message = Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1), () => 'three (one second later)');

  // 2. the search as you type
  Timer? _debounce;
  int _requestNumber = 0; // the number of the LAST search launched
  List<String> _results = [];

  void _trace(String message) => setState(() => _log.add('${currentTime()} $message'));

  // called on each keystroke
  void _onInput(String text) {
    // the DEBOUNCE: each keystroke cancels the timer of the previous
    // keystroke; the search only starts after 400 ms without a keystroke
    _debounce?.cancel();
    _debounce = Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 400), () => _launch(text.trim().toLowerCase()));
  }

  Future<void> _launch(String text) async {
    // fewer than two letters: no search, no result
    if (text.length < 2) {
      _requestNumber++; // a response still expected will be ignored
      setState(() => _results = []);
      return;
    }
    // "stale": a response that arrives AFTER another search has been
    // launched must be ignored (otherwise the slow response of an old
    // search would overwrite the one of the new one)
    final number = ++_requestNumber;
    _trace('search sent: "$text"');
    final found = await search(text);
    if (!mounted) return;
    if (number != _requestNumber) {
      _trace('response ignored (stale): "$text"');
      return;
    }
    setState(() => _results = found);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _debounce?.cancel();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final titleStyle = Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleSmall;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Example 19 - asynchrony')),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        children: [
          Card(
            child: Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
              child: Column(
                crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                children: [
                  Text('A countdown (a Stream and StreamBuilder)', style: titleStyle),
                  // StreamBuilder: rebuilds its content on each value of the Stream;
                  // snapshot.data: the last value received (null before the first one)
                  StreamBuilder<int>(
                    stream: _countdown,
                    builder: (context, snapshot) =>
                        Text(snapshot.hasData ? '${snapshot.data}' : '...', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.displaySmall),
                  ),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ),
          Card(
            child: Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
              child: Column(
                crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                children: [
                  Text('A search as you type (debounce, stale responses)', style: titleStyle),
                  TextField(
                    decoration: const InputDecoration(hintText: 'at least two letters: pel, dur...'),
                    onChanged: _onInput,
                  ),
                  for (final r in _results) Text('• $r'),
                  if (_results.isEmpty) const Text('no result', style: TextStyle(color: Colors.grey)),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ),
          Card(
            child: Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
              child: Column(
                crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                children: [
                  Text('Waiting for a Future (FutureBuilder)', style: titleStyle),
                  // as long as the Future is not complete: the waiting content
                  FutureBuilder<String>(
                    future: _message,
                    builder: (context, snapshot) => switch (snapshot.connectionState) {
                      ConnectionState.done => Text('received: ${snapshot.data}'),
                      _ => const Text('waiting...', style: TextStyle(color: Colors.grey)),
                    },
                  ),
                ],
              ),
            ),
          ),
          Text('Log', style: titleStyle),
          for (final (i, line) in _log.indexed) Text('${i + 1}. $line', style: const TextStyle(fontSize: 12)),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • lines 24–26: a simulated “server”: a function [async], whose response (a [Future]) arrives after a random delay. [await Future<void>.delayed(...)] waits for this delay without blocking the application;
  • lines 31–34: a [Stream] generated by a function [async*] (with an asterisk): an asynchronous generator. Each [yield] sends a value to those listening to [Stream]; between values, the function waits one second;
  • lines 61–63: the [Stream] and the [Future] are created ONCE, in fields of the [State] object, and not in [build]: each rebuild would restart the countdown! This is the most common error with [FutureBuilder] and [StreamBuilder];
  • lines 66–68: the status of the search as the user types: a timer, the number of the last search initiated, and the results;
  • lines 73–77: debouncing: the program waits for the user to pause before querying the server, rather than sending a request with every keystroke. Each keystroke resets the timer from the previous keystroke ([cancel()]) and starts a new one: the search is only triggered after 400 milliseconds without a keystroke;
  • Lines 80–98: the search. An “out-of-date” response (one that arrives AFTER another search has been launched) must be ignored: otherwise, the slow response from an old search would override that of the new one. Each search is assigned a number ([++_requestNumber]); when its response arrives, if it is no longer the number of the most recent search, it is ignored. [if (!mounted) return;]: the screen may have disappeared while waiting;
  • lines 102–104: the timer is stopped if the screen disappears;
  • lines 124–127: [StreamBuilder] listens for [Stream] and reconstructs its content with each new value. [builder] receives a snapshot ([snapshot], an [AsyncSnapshot]): [snapshot.hasData], [snapshot.data] (the last value received), [snapshot.hasError], [snapshot.connectionState]. When the widget disappears, [StreamBuilder] unsubscribes on its own;
  • lines 158–162: [FutureBuilder] waits for [Future]: until it is finished, the placeholder content; then, its value. [switch] on [snapshot.connectionState] chooses one or the other.

We type “p,” “pe,” “pel” quickly: only one search is sent. Then “du,” followed by “dup” before the response: the response to “du” arrives too late, and it is ignored if “dup” has already received its response:

In [JavaScript], the same thing is written using promises and timers; [Angular] adds the "observables" from [RxJS]. In [Dart], [Future] and [Stream] are in the base library, and [async], [await], [async*], [yield], and [await for] are in the language: this is why [Flutter] does not require a library for asynchronous operations.

docs.title: 6.2. Example 20: A Shared State
docs.text:
Same question as in previous lessons: what are the “scopes” for an application’s data?

  • A widget’s local state disappears when the widget is removed;
  • the state of a “store” is shared by all widgets and survives their removal… but not the application’s shutdown;
  • State stored on the device survives when the application is shut down.

docs.title: 6.2.1. The shopping cart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/ex20_shared_state/stores/cart.dart - a SHARED STATE, with provider
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A "store" is a state that lives OUTSIDE the screens, in a SINGLE
// instance, shared by all those who read it. Example 14 did it
// by hand (InheritedNotifier); the provider package, the most used
// with Flutter (and recommended by its documentation), does the same thing
// in one line:
//
//     ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Cart(), child: ...)
//
// The store is an ordinary ChangeNotifier. Usual organization:
//   - the STATE: PRIVATE data (_items);
//   - the ACTIONS: methods, the only ones to modify the state, which end
//     with notifyListeners();
//   - the computed values: getters.
// A widget accesses it through its context:
//   - context.watch<Cart>()  : read AND subscribe (rebuilt on each change);
//   - context.read<Cart>()   : read without subscribing (to call an action);
//   - context.select<Cart, int>((p) => p.count) : subscribe to ONE value:
//     rebuilt only if THIS value changes.
// The store lives as long as its provider lives: it survives the removal of a
// screen... but not the stopping of the application.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

typedef Item = ({String label, double price});

class Cart extends ChangeNotifier {
  final List<Item> _items = [];

  // a NON-MODIFIABLE view of the list: only the actions change it
  List<Item> get items => List.unmodifiable(_items);
  int get count => _items.length;
  double get total => _items.fold(0, (s, a) => s + a.price);

  void add(Item item) {
    _items.add(item);
    notifyListeners();
  }

  void clear() {
    _items.clear();
    notifyListeners();
  }
}

A store is a state that spans multiple screens, existing as a single instance shared by all who access it. Example 14 implemented this manually. The [provider] package, the most commonly used one along with [Flutter] (and the one recommended in its documentation), does the same thing in a single line: [ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Cart(), child: ...)].

  • Line 31: the state: private data;
  • lines 34–36: calculated values: getters. [List.unmodifiable]: a read-only view of the list; only actions can modify it;
  • lines 38–45: the actions: methods—the only ones that modify the state—which end with [notifyListeners()].

docs.title: 6.2.2. Preferences
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/ex20_shared_state/stores/preferences.dart - a state that survives the stopping
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// For a piece of data to survive the stopping of the application, it must be stored
// ON THE DEVICE. The shared_preferences package offers a small dictionary
// key -> value (bool, int, double, String), specific to the application and
// kept on the device (on the web: in the browser's localStorage).
//   - at startup, the stored values are read (main.dart);
//   - on each change, they are written again.
// NEVER store sensitive data there (password, token): they are
// written in clear text.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

class Preferences extends ChangeNotifier {
  static const _darkKey = 'example20.dark';
  static const _sizeKey = 'example20.size';

  final SharedPreferences _storage;
  bool _dark;
  double _size; // size of the text

  // the initial state: what the device has stored, otherwise the default values
  Preferences(this._storage)
    : _dark = _storage.getBool(_darkKey) ?? false,
      _size = _storage.getDouble(_sizeKey) ?? 16;

  bool get dark => _dark;
  double get size => _size;

  // one optional named parameter per preference: only what is provided changes
  void update({bool? dark, double? size}) {
    if (dark != null) {
      _dark = dark;
      _storage.setBool(_darkKey, dark); // writing on the device
    }
    if (size != null) {
      _size = size;
      _storage.setDouble(_sizeKey, size);
    }
    notifyListeners();
  }
}

For data to survive after the application is shut down, it must be stored on the device. The [shared_preferences] package provides a small key->value dictionary ([bool], [int], [double], [String]), specific to the application and stored on the device (on the web: in the browser’s [localStorage]).

  • Line 21: the storage data, received upon creation;
  • lines 26–28: the initial state: what the device has stored, or default values otherwise. The fields are initialized by the constructor’s “initialization list” (after the colon), before the body;
  • Lines 34–43: a single action, with optional named parameters: only the provided values are changed, and they are immediately written to the device ([setBool], [setDouble]).

NEVER store any sensitive data (passwords, tokens) there: such data is written in plain text. For this purpose, there is the [flutter_secure_storage] package, which uses the system’s vault ([Keystore] from [Android], [Keychain] from [iOS]).

docs.title: 6.2.3. The widgets
docs.text:
// lib/ex20_shared_state/components/shop.dart - ADDS to the shared cart
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import '../stores/cart.dart';

const products = <Item>[(label: 'Consultation', price: 30), (label: 'Vaccine', price: 12.5)];

class Shop extends StatelessWidget {
  const Shop({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // read: we only CALL an action; Shop is not
    // rebuilt when the cart changes
    final cart = context.read<Cart>();
    return Card(
      child: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
          children: [
            Text('Shop', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleSmall),
            for (final p in products)
              TextButton.icon(
                icon: const Icon(Icons.add),
                label: Text('${p.label} (${p.price} €)'),
                onPressed: () => cart.add(p),
              ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • Line 16: [context.read<Cart>()] reads the shopping cart provided above; WITHOUT subscribing: the store simply calls an action; it does not need to be rebuilt when the shopping cart changes. 
// lib/ex20_shared_state/components/cart_summary.dart - READS the same cart
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import '../stores/cart.dart';

class CartSummary extends StatelessWidget {
  const CartSummary({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // select: rebuilds ONLY if the count or the total changes
    final count = context.select<Cart, int>((p) => p.count);
    final total = context.select<Cart, double>((p) => p.total);
    return Card(
      child: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        child: Row(
          children: [
            const Icon(Icons.shopping_cart),
            const SizedBox(width: 8),
            Expanded(child: Text('$count item(s), $total €')),
            TextButton(
              onPressed: count == 0 ? null : () => context.read<Cart>().clear(),
              child: const Text('Clear'),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • Lines 13–14: [context.select] reads ONE value of the shopping cart and subscribes the widget to THAT value: it is rebuilt only if that value changes. [context.watch<Cart>()] would read and subscribe to the entire shopping cart. 
// lib/ex20_shared_state/components/local_counter.dart - a LOCAL state, which disappears with the widget
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class LocalCounter extends StatefulWidget {
  final String title;

  const LocalCounter({super.key, required this.title});

  @override
  State<LocalCounter> createState() => _LocalCounterState();
}

class _LocalCounterState extends State<LocalCounter> {
  int _clicks = 0;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Card(
      child: ListTile(
        title: Text(widget.title),
        trailing: OutlinedButton(onPressed: () => setState(() => _clicks++), child: Text('$_clicks click(s)')),
      ),
    );
  }
}

A local state that disappears with the widget.

docs.title: 6.2.4. The application
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/ex20_shared_state/main.dart - three "scopes" of data
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//   - the LOCAL state of a widget (LocalCounter) disappears with it;
//   - the state of a STORE (the cart) is shared by all the widgets
//     and survives their removal - but not the stopping of the application;
//   - the state stored on the device (the preferences) survives the stopping.
// And Visibility(maintainState: true): the content is HIDDEN, but not
// removed; its local state is kept.
// Uncheck then check again "show the area", then stop and restart
// the application: compare.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

import 'components/shop.dart';
import 'components/local_counter.dart';
import 'components/cart_summary.dart';
import 'stores/cart.dart';
import 'stores/preferences.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // essential before using a "plugin" (code specific to Android, iOS,
  // web...) like shared_preferences, BEFORE runApp
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  final storage = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  runApp(
    // MultiProvider: several providers, nested in one another,
    // above the whole application
    MultiProvider(
      providers: [
        ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Cart()),
        ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Preferences(storage)),
      ],
      child: const Application(),
    ),
  );
}

class Application extends StatelessWidget {
  const Application({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // watch: the application is rebuilt when the preferences change
    final preferences = context.watch<Preferences>();
    return MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      // the dark theme, and the choice between the two
      darkTheme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo, brightness: Brightness.dark),
      themeMode: preferences.dark ? ThemeMode.dark : ThemeMode.light,
      // builder: wraps ALL the screens; here, the size of the text
      builder: (context, child) => MediaQuery(
        data: MediaQuery.of(context).copyWith(textScaler: TextScaler.linear(preferences.size / 16)),
        child: child!,
      ),
      home: const SharedStatePage(),
    );
  }
}

class SharedStatePage extends StatefulWidget {
  const SharedStatePage({super.key});

  @override
  State<SharedStatePage> createState() => _SharedStatePageState();
}

class _SharedStatePageState extends State<SharedStatePage> {
  bool _areaVisible = true;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final preferences = context.watch<Preferences>();
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Example 20 - a shared state')),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        children: [
          SwitchListTile(
            title: const Text('dark theme'),
            value: preferences.dark,
            onChanged: (v) => preferences.update(dark: v),
          ),
          ListTile(
            title: Text('text size: ${preferences.size.round()}'),
            subtitle: Slider(
              value: preferences.size,
              min: 12,
              max: 22,
              divisions: 10,
              onChanged: (v) => preferences.update(size: v),
            ),
          ),
          CheckboxListTile(
            title: const Text('show the area'),
            value: _areaVisible,
            onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _areaVisible = v!),
          ),
          // removed: these widgets disappear, with their local state
          if (_areaVisible) ...[const Shop(), const CartSummary(), const LocalCounter(title: 'Local state')],
          // hidden: the widget stays in memory, its state is kept
          Visibility(
            visible: _areaVisible,
            maintainState: true,
            child: const LocalCounter(title: 'Local state, in a Visibility'),
          ),
          const Padding(
            padding: EdgeInsets.symmetric(vertical: 8),
            child: Text('Outside the area, a second summary of the SAME cart (it stays there when the area disappears):'),
          ),
          const CartSummary(),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • Lines 27–28: [shared_preferences] is a "plugin": it uses platform-specific code ([Android], web...). To use it BEFORE [runApp], you must first initialize [Flutter] ([ensureInitialized]). Reading from storage is asynchronous: [main] waits for it to complete;
  • lines 32–35: [MultiProvider] places multiple providers, one inside the other, at the top of the entire application. [ChangeNotifierProvider] creates [ChangeNotifier] ([create]), provides it to its descendants, rebuilds those that subscribe to it when it changes, and releases it when it disappears;
  • line 48: the application reads the preferences and subscribes to them; it is rebuilt when they change;
  • lines 53–54: two themes, light and dark, and the option to choose between them ([themeMode]);
  • lines 56–58: the [builder] from [MaterialApp] wraps ALL the screens. Here, the text size for the entire app is changed: [MediaQuery] describes the screen and the user’s settings (including [textScaler], the text magnification factor, which can also be adjusted in the phone’s accessibility settings);
  • line 104: removed; the area disappears, along with the local state of its widgets;
  • Lines 106–109: [Visibility] with [maintainState: true] HIDES its child without removing it: its state is preserved. (This is what [<Activity mode="hidden">] does in the [React] course.)

We add two items, click once on each local counter (on the left); we remove the area and switch to dark mode (in the middle); we restore the area (on the right):

The shopping cart survived the removal of the section (as shown in the second summary); the removed counter reset to zero; the hidden counter retained its value. Stop the app and restart it: the dark theme and text size are preserved, and the shopping cart is empty.

Why [provider]? There are many state management libraries for [Flutter] ([Riverpod], [Bloc], [GetX], [MobX]...). [provider] is the simplest: it is simply a convenient way to write the [InheritedWidget] from Example 14, based on the [ChangeNotifier] from [Flutter]. This is the one used in the architecture guide for the [Flutter] documentation, and the one that will be used in the case study.

docs.title: 11. Case Study: The Flutter client for the RdvMedecins application
11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The [RdvMedecins] app allows users to schedule appointments at a doctor's office. The [NestJS] course developed it as a HTML application, in which the server generated the pages; the [Vue.js], [Angular], and [React] wrote web clients for it, which generate the SAME pages in the browser, based on the JSON data from the server presented in the chapter “The RdvMedecins Server, a Black Box.” Here we describe the [Flutter] client: a mobile application ([Android]), which can also be compiled for the web.

The client must provide everything the others did:

  • a login screen, protected by a CAPTCHA, with the option to create a patient account;
  • a doctor’s schedule for a given day, with appointment booking (patient selection window) and cancellation;
  • for the administrator, management of doctors and clients (list, add, edit, delete);
  • for the patient, a personal dashboard (showing upcoming appointments, which they can cancel) and account management;
  • two languages: French and English;
  • the same addresses as the web clients ([/schedule?doctorId=1&day=...]). On the phone, they are invisible but organize the app; on the web, users can reload them, bookmark them, and navigate the app using the browser’s Back/Forward buttons.

A mobile app adds its own requirements: a narrow screen (no five-column tables), a keyboard that hides half the screen, a Back button, a password manager, and the absence of a browser to store the token cookie.

docs.title: 11.2. Installation and Execution
docs.text:
The JSON server must be installed and running (see the chapter “The RdvMedecins Server: A Black Box”). You do not need the CAPTCHA test mode: you can leave the [CAPTCHA_TEST] field blank in the [.env] file on the server.

In a console window open to the [rdvmedecins_flutter] folder:

flutter create --platforms=android,web --org fr.stahe --project-name rdvmedecins_flutter .
flutter pub get

The first command adds the platform-specific folders ([android/], [web/]) to the project, as in the examples; it does not modify any existing files, and the delivered [android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml] file (the one from Example 22) is retained. Then, choose one of the following:

flutter run -d emulator-5554
flutter run -d R58N12ABCDE --dart-define=SERVER=http://192.168.1.20:8080
flutter run -d chrome
  • The first line launches the application on the [Android] emulator (the [flutter devices] command lists the available devices). The emulator connects to the server at the address [10.0.2.2:8080] (see Example 22);
  • the second line runs the app on a real phone connected via USB (with “USB debugging” enabled in its developer options) or connected via Wi-Fi. The phone and computer must be on the same network; enter the computer’s address on this network ([ipconfig] under [Windows]). The firewall on [Windows] must allow incoming connections on port 8080;
  • the third, on [Chrome], at the address http://localhost:5173: the web development server in [Flutter] forwards /api requests to the JSON server (file [web_dev_config.yaml]).

The demo accounts are listed on the login screen (password = login). While the application is running, the [r] key on the console performs a "hot reload" after a code change; [R] restarts it; [q] stops it.

docs.title: 11.4. Client Architecture
docs.text:
rdvmedecins_flutter/
├── pubspec.yaml               the libraries, the resources
├── analysis_options.yaml      the rules of the code analyzer
├── web_dev_config.yaml        the web development server (proxy /api)
├── android/                   the Android project (including AndroidManifest.xml)
├── web/                       the HTML page of the web version
├── assets/
│   ├── i18n/                  the dictionaries fr.json, en.json
│   └── fonts/                 the RobotoMono font
├── test/                      unit tests; making of the screenshots
└── lib/
    ├── main.dart              the startup
    ├── config.dart            the server address
    ├── router.dart            the screens, their addresses, their access rights
    ├── formatting.dart        the formatting of times and days
    ├── api/                   the API access layer
    ├── i18n/                  the languages
    ├── state/                 session, messages, cache (ChangeNotifier)
    ├── widgets/               the layout and the reusable widgets
    └── pages/                 the screens

This is the architecture recommended by the [Flutter] guide (“App architecture”), explained more simply:

  • a data layer ([api/]): the only layer that knows the [http] package, the URLs, and the JSON;
  • a state layer ([state/]): [ChangeNotifier] objects provided to the entire application ([provider]), which the screens monitor;
  • an interface layer ([pages/], [widgets/]): widgets that display the state and transmit user actions.

The following table compares the HTML application from the [NestJS] course, the [React] client, and this client:

All of the client’s files are presented below. They are extensively commented; their comments are part of the course.

docs.title: 11.6.1. lib/config.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/config.dart - WHERE is the JSON server?
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The question does not arise for a web application served by the
// server itself: the requests go to the SAME origin as the page
// (a relative address, /api/...). But a MOBILE application has no
// origin: it must be given the full address of the server.
//   - the Android emulator sees the computer that runs it at
//     the address 10.0.2.2 (localhost, for it, is the emulator itself);
//   - a real phone, connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the computer, must
//     use the address of the computer on this network (192.168.1.20...):
//     it is given when the application is launched:
//         flutter run --dart-define=SERVER=http://192.168.1.20:8080 ...
//   - in web development (flutter run -d chrome), Flutter's development
//     server forwards the /api requests to the JSON server
//     (web_dev_config.yaml file): a relative address is enough;
//   - on a computer (Windows, macOS, Linux): localhost.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

// the value given by --dart-define=SERVER=..., '' by default.
// String.fromEnvironment is evaluated at COMPILE time: it is a constant
const _forcedServer = String.fromEnvironment('SERVER');

class Config {
  // kIsWeb: true if the application runs in a browser;
  // defaultTargetPlatform: the system (android, iOS, windows...)
  static String serverUrl = _forcedServer.isNotEmpty
      ? _forcedServer
      : kIsWeb
      ? '' // same origin: relative addresses
      : defaultTargetPlatform == TargetPlatform.android
      ? 'http://10.0.2.2:8080'
      : 'http://localhost:8080';
}

The server address, depending on the platform (see Example 22):

  • line 24: the value provided at launch by [--dart-define=SERVER=...]. [String.fromEnvironment] is evaluated at compile time: the address is embedded in the built application;
  • lines 29–35: otherwise, a relative address on the web (the development server, then the JSON server itself in production, serve the page AND the API), [10.0.2.2] on [Android] (the computer, as seen from the emulator), [localhost] elsewhere. [static]: a class variable, not an object variable; not [final], so that the tests can modify it.

docs.title: 11.6.2. lib/main.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/main.dart - the startup of the application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// We build, once and for all, the objects shared by the whole
// application, then we PROVIDE them to all the screens (provider):
//   - the HTTP client (which handles the token cookie on the phone) and the
//     API access layer;
//   - the session (who is logged in?), the messages, the data cache;
//   - the translations (French, English);
//   - the router, which displays the screen of the current address.
// Two mechanisms link these objects together:
//   1. the 401 response of a protected request (session expired): we forget
//      the user and prepare the message; the router, which listens to the
//      session, then goes back to the login screen (see api/api_client.dart);
//   2. the "flash" messages: at the end of EACH navigation, the messages
//      of the previous screen disappear, those left for the next
//      screen appear (see state/messages.dart).
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_localizations/flutter_localizations.dart';
import 'package:flutter_web_plugins/url_strategy.dart';
import 'package:go_router/go_router.dart';
import 'package:intl/date_symbol_data_local.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

import 'api/api_client.dart';
import 'api/http_client.dart';
import 'api/rdvmedecins_api.dart';
import 'state/cache.dart';
import 'state/messages.dart';
import 'state/session.dart';
import 'i18n/translations.dart';
import 'router.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  usePathUrlStrategy(); // on the web: /schedule rather than /#/schedule
  await initializeDateFormatting();
  final storage = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  final translations = Translations(storage);
  await translations.start();
  runApp(Application(storage: storage, translations: translations));
}

class Application extends StatefulWidget {
  final SharedPreferences storage;
  final Translations translations;

  const Application({super.key, required this.storage, required this.translations});

  @override
  State<Application> createState() => _ApplicationState();
}

class _ApplicationState extends State<Application> {
  late final ApiClient _client = ApiClient(CookieClient(widget.storage));
  late final RdvMedecinsApi _api = RdvMedecinsApi(_client);
  late final Session _session = Session(_api);
  final Messages _messages = Messages();
  final Cache _cache = Cache();
  late final GoRouter _router = createRouter(_session, _messages, _api);
  String? _address;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    // 1. the expired session
    _client.onSessionExpired = () {
      _session.forget();
      _cache.clear();
      _messages.flash(success: false, key: 'ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED');
      // no _router.go('/login'): the router's guard takes care of it, and
      // remembers the current screen (?redirect=...) to come back to it
    };
    // the session changes (login, logout): the data read for
    // the previous user are no longer worth anything
    _session.addListener(_cache.clear);
    // 2. at each completed navigation (the address has changed): new page
    _router.routerDelegate.addListener(() {
      // state: the screen at the TOP of the stack (including a screen pushed by push)
      final address = _router.state.uri.toString();
      if (address != _address) {
        _address = address;
        _messages.newPage();
      }
    });
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _router.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MultiProvider(
      providers: [
        // ordinary objects...
        Provider.value(value: _api),
        // ... and objects that notify their changes
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: _cache),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: _session),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: _messages),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: widget.translations),
      ],
      child: Consumer<Translations>(
        builder: (context, translations, _) => MaterialApp.router(
          debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
          onGenerateTitle: (context) => translations.t('APP.TITLE'),
          theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: const Color(0xFF0D6EFD)),
          // the texts of Flutter itself (calendar...) in the chosen language
          locale: Locale(translations.language),
          supportedLocales: [for (final l in languages) Locale(l)],
          localizationsDelegates: GlobalMaterialLocalizations.delegates,
          routerConfig: _router,
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • lines 37–44: Before displaying anything, we prepare what needs to be prepared: web addresses without [#] (example 17), the names of days and months in all languages ([intl], example 09), the device’s storage, and the initial language's dictionary. [WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized()]: These operations require the [Flutter] engine, so we start it before [runApp];
  • lines 58–63: the shared objects, created ONCE, in the root widget’s state. Each receives the ones it needs upon creation: this is dependency injection, done manually. [late]: Initialization occurs upon first use, when [widget] already exists;
  • lines 70–76: 1. the expired session. The API access layer is unaware of either the session or the messages; it is entrusted with this function, which it will call upon every 401 response. The user is forgotten, the cache is cleared, and the message for the next screen is prepared. The screen transition itself is handled by the router, which monitors the session;
  • line 79: every time the user changes, the cache is cleared: the data read for the previous user is of no use to the next one (a patient should not see the calendar viewed by the administrator);
  • Lines 81–88: 2. Flash messages. The router’s [routerDelegate] alerts its listeners with each transmission; the address is compared to the previous one ([_router.state]: the screen at the TOP of the stack, including a screen stacked by [push], such as the reservation window), and, if it has changed, the system moves to a “new page”: the messages from the previous screen disappear, and those placed on this one appear (see [messages.dart]);
  • lines 99–107: shared objects are provided to all screens (Example 20). [.value]: the object already exists; the provider does not create it (and will not destroy it);
  • lines 109–118: the application itself, rebuilt with every language change ([Consumer], see Example 20): the title ([onGenerateTitle]), and the language of the text in [Flutter] itself (the calendar, tooltips). [colorSchemeSeed]: a color from which [Material] derives the entire palette; this is the blue of [Bootstrap], the color used by web clients.

docs.title: 11.7. The access layer to the API
11.7.1. lib/api/http_client.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/api/http_client.dart - an HTTP client that handles COOKIES
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The RdvMedecins server puts the JWT token in a COOKIE (httpOnly).
// In a browser, it is the browser that stores the cookies and sends them
// back with each request: the application code has nothing to do.
// On a phone, there is NO browser: it is up to the application to
// play its role, that is:
//   1. read the "Set-Cookie" header of each response, and store the cookies;
//   2. send them back in the "Cookie" header of each request.
// This HTTP client does it, by WRAPPING the client of the http package
// (http.BaseClient: writing the send method is enough). The cookies are
// also stored on the device (shared_preferences): we stay logged in
// when we stop and restart the application.
// On the web, it does nothing more than the ordinary client: the
// browser forbids the application to read or write these headers.
// =========================================================================

import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

class CookieClient extends http.BaseClient {
  static const _key = 'rdvmedecins.cookies';

  final http.Client _inner = http.Client();
  final SharedPreferences? _storage;
  // cookie name -> its value
  final Map<String, String> _cookies = {};

  CookieClient([this._storage]) {
    // the cookies stored during a previous use
    final stored = _storage?.getString(_key);
    if (stored != null) {
      _cookies.addAll((jsonDecode(stored) as Map<String, Object?>).cast<String, String>());
    }
  }

  @override
  Future<http.StreamedResponse> send(http.BaseRequest request) async {
    if (!kIsWeb && _cookies.isNotEmpty) {
      // "rdvmedecins_jwt=eyJhbGci...; other=value"
      request.headers['cookie'] = [for (final MapEntry(:key, :value) in _cookies.entries) '$key=$value'].join('; ');
    }
    final response = await _inner.send(request);
    final setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
    if (!kIsWeb && setCookie != null) {
      _store(setCookie);
    }
    return response;
  }

  // Set-Cookie: rdvmedecins_jwt=eyJ...; Max-Age=7200; Path=/api; Expires=Tue, 29 Sep 2026 ...; HttpOnly
  // (several cookies are separated by commas). We only keep the
  // name and the value of each cookie; an empty value (logout) deletes it
  void _store(String setCookie) {
    // a name followed by "=", at the start of the header or after a comma
    for (final m in RegExp(r'(?:^|,)\s*([^=;,\s]+)=([^;]*)').allMatches(setCookie)) {
      final name = m[1]!;
      final value = m[2]!.trim();
      if (value.isEmpty) {
        _cookies.remove(name);
      } else {
        _cookies[name] = value;
      }
    }
    _storage?.setString(_key, jsonEncode(_cookies));
  }

  @override
  void close() => _inner.close();
}

The HTTP client from Example 23, unchanged: it stores the received cookies ([Set-Cookie] header) and sends them back ([Cookie] header) to the phone; on the web, it lets the browser handle it.

docs.title: 11.7.2. lib/api/api_client.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/api/api_client.dart - ALL the requests to the API go through here
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Taken from common/api.dart of the examples, with something new: the
// centralized handling of the 401 response.
//
// A 401 can happen at any time: the token has expired (2 hours), the
// account has been deleted, the server has restarted with another secret
// key... Rather than handling this case in each screen, we handle it
// HERE, once. But this file knows neither the router nor the messages
// (it depends on nothing): it calls a function that was given to it at
// startup (onSessionExpired, see main.dart), which forgets the user and
// goes back to the login page.
//
// Some requests handle their 401 themselves (the login, GET
// /api/auth/me...): they are "public" (see rdvmedecins_api.dart).
// =========================================================================

import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

import '../config.dart';
import 'api_error.dart';

class ApiClient {
  final http.Client _client;
  // what to do when the server responds 401 to a protected request
  void Function() onSessionExpired = () {};

  ApiClient(this._client);

  // isPublic: true for the routes that handle the 401 themselves
  Future<Object?> request(String method, String url, {Object? body, bool isPublic = false}) async {
    final request = http.Request(method, Uri.parse('${Config.serverUrl}/api$url'));
    if (body != null) {
      request.headers['content-type'] = 'application/json';
      request.body = jsonEncode(body);
    }
    final http.Response response;
    try {
      response = await http.Response.fromStream(await _client.send(request));
    } catch (_) {
      // no response: network down, server stopped, wrong address
      throw const ApiError(0, 'ERRORS.SERVER_UNREACHABLE');
    }
    if (response.statusCode >= 400) {
      final error = ApiError.fromResponse(response);
      if (error.statusCode == 401 && !isPublic) {
        onSessionExpired();
        // the screen that was waiting for the response will display THIS message too
        throw const ApiError(401, 'ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED');
      }
      throw error;
    }
    return response.bodyBytes.isEmpty ? null : jsonDecode(utf8.decode(response.bodyBytes));
  }
}

The [common/api.dart] file from the examples, with a new feature: the 401 response.

  • Line 29: a function to call in the event of a 401 error, specified at startup (see [main.dart]). By default, it does nothing;
  • line 34: [isPublic] is a named, optional parameter (enclosed in curly braces): [request('GET', '/captcha', isPublic: true)];
  • lines 35–38: the request, built piece by piece: method, address, header, and JSON body;
  • lines 40–45: the request is sent. An exception here means that no response was received (network down, server down, incorrect address). [final http.Response response;]: a variable [final] declared without a value; [Dart] checks that it receives a value—only once—before being read;
  • lines 47–54: an error response becomes an [ApiError]. A 401 on a protected request means the session has expired: [onSessionExpired] is called, then an error is triggered anyway (the screen that was waiting for the response must know that it did not arrive), using the key [ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED]: if this screen displays the error, it is the same message;
  • line 56: a response with no body (204) yields [null]. We decode the bytes to UTF-8: without the header [charset], the [http] package would decode [response.body] in Latin-1, and the accents would be corrupted.

docs.title: 11.7.3. lib/api/api_error.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/api/api_error.dart - ONE class for all the errors of the API
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// All the error responses of the RdvMedecins server have the same shape:
//   { "statusCode": 409, "key": "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN", "params": {...}, "fields": {...} }
// But a request can also fail OTHERWISE: no response at all
// (network down, server stopped, wrong address), or a response that does not
// come from our server (an error page of a proxy). We convert
// all of this into ONE class, ApiError, which carries the translation key
// sent by the server (and, if there are any, its parameters and the error of
// each field).
// =========================================================================

import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

// "implements Exception": an object that can be thrown (throw) and caught (catch)
class ApiError implements Exception {
  final int statusCode; // 0: the server did not respond
  final String key; // e.g. 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN'
  final Map<String, String> params;
  final Map<String, String> fields;

  const ApiError(this.statusCode, this.key, {this.params = const {}, this.fields = const {}});

  // an error response (4xx, 5xx) -> an ApiError
  factory ApiError.fromResponse(http.Response response) {
    Object? body;
    try {
      body = jsonDecode(utf8.decode(response.bodyBytes));
    } on FormatException {
      body = null; // not JSON: it is not our server that responded
    }
    // the "pattern matching" of a Map: if the body has a key
    // "key" of type String, it is stored in the variable key
    if (body case {'key': final String key}) {
      final json = body as Map<String, Object?>;
      return ApiError(response.statusCode, key, params: _strings(json['params']), fields: _strings(json['fields']));
    }
    // no key: the proxy or the network responded in its place
    return ApiError(
      response.statusCode,
      response.statusCode >= 500 ? 'ERRORS.SERVER_UNREACHABLE' : 'ERRORS.SERVER_ERROR',
    );
  }

  // a JSON object { "name": "ERRORS..." } -> Map<String, String> (empty otherwise)
  static Map<String, String> _strings(Object? json) =>
      json is Map<String, Object?> ? {for (final e in json.entries) e.key: '${e.value}'} : const {};

  @override
  String toString() => '$statusCode $key';
}

The one from Example 24: any request that fails ends with an [ApiError], which contains the message’s translation key, its parameters, and the error for each field.

docs.title: 11.7.4. lib/api/types.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/api/types.dart - the JSON objects exchanged with the server
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The translation, into Dart classes, of the API described in the chapter "The
// server, a black box" (see common/types.dart of the examples). Each
// class reads its JSON with Dart 3 pattern matching: a response that does not
// have the expected shape is detected as soon as it is received.
// =========================================================================

enum Role { admin, doctor, user }

Role _role(String name) => Role.values.byName(name.toLowerCase());

Never _unexpected(String what, Object? json) => throw FormatException('unexpected $what: $json');

// POST /api/auth/login, GET /api/auth/me, PUT /api/my-account
class User {
  final String login;
  final String name; // displayed name: "Marie PELISSIER"
  final Role role;

  const User(this.login, this.name, this.role);

  factory User.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'login': final String login, 'name': final String name, 'role': final String role} => User(
      login,
      name,
      _role(role),
    ),
    _ => _unexpected('User', json),
  };
}

// GET /api/captcha
class Captcha {
  final String id;
  final String svg;

  const Captcha(this.id, this.svg);

  factory Captcha.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'id': final String id, 'svg': final String svg} => Captcha(id, svg),
    _ => _unexpected('Captcha', json),
  };
}

// a title, a first name, a last name
class Identity {
  final String title;
  final String firstName;
  final String lastName;

  const Identity(this.title, this.firstName, this.lastName);

  factory Identity.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'title': final String title, 'firstName': final String firstName, 'lastName': final String lastName} => Identity(
      title,
      firstName,
      lastName,
    ),
    _ => _unexpected('Identity', json),
  };

  // "Mme Alice DURAND"
  String get label => '$title $firstName $lastName';
}

// a doctor or a client: GET /api/doctors, GET /api/clients/:id...
class Person extends Identity {
  final int id;
  final int version; // optimistic lock: to be sent back with an update
  final String? login; // only for the ADMIN

  const Person(this.id, this.version, super.title, super.firstName, super.lastName, [this.login]);

  factory Person.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {
      'id': final int id,
      'version': final int version,
      'title': final String title,
      'firstName': final String firstName,
      'lastName': final String lastName,
    } =>
      Person(id, version, title, firstName, lastName, (json as Map<String, Object?>)['login'] as String?),
    _ => _unexpected('Person', json),
  };

  static List<Person> list(Object? json) => [for (final p in json as List<Object?>) Person.fromJson(p)];
}

// a time slot
class Slot {
  final int id;
  final int startHour;
  final int startMinute;
  final int endHour;
  final int endMinute;

  const Slot(this.id, this.startHour, this.startMinute, this.endHour, this.endMinute);

  factory Slot.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'id': final int id, 'startHour': final int sh, 'startMinute': final int sm, 'endHour': final int eh, 'endMinute': final int em} =>
      Slot(id, sh, sm, eh, em),
    _ => _unexpected('Slot', json),
  };
}

// a line of the schedule, with the RIGHTS of the logged-in user
class ScheduleSlot extends Slot {
  final bool free;
  final Identity? patient; // null: free, or taken by another patient
  final bool mine; // the logged-in patient's appointment
  final bool bookable;
  final int? appointmentId; // set if the user can cancel

  const ScheduleSlot(
    super.id,
    super.startHour,
    super.startMinute,
    super.endHour,
    super.endMinute,
    this.free,
    this.patient,
    this.mine,
    this.bookable,
    this.appointmentId,
  );

  factory ScheduleSlot.fromJson(Object? json) {
    final s = Slot.fromJson(json);
    return switch (json) {
      {
        'free': final bool free,
        'patient': final Object? patient,
        'mine': final bool mine,
        'bookable': final bool bookable,
        'appointmentId': final int? appointmentId,
      } =>
        ScheduleSlot(
          s.id,
          s.startHour,
          s.startMinute,
          s.endHour,
          s.endMinute,
          free,
          patient == null ? null : Identity.fromJson(patient),
          mine,
          bookable,
          appointmentId,
        ),
      _ => _unexpected('Slot', json),
    };
  }
}

// GET /api/schedule?doctorId=...&day=...
class Schedule {
  final Person doctor;
  final String day; // "yyyy-MM-dd"
  final List<ScheduleSlot> slots;
  final String? info; // translation key (patient who already has an appointment)

  const Schedule(this.doctor, this.day, this.slots, this.info);

  factory Schedule.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {
      'doctor': final Object doctor,
      'day': final String day,
      'slots': final List<Object?> slots,
      'info': final String? info,
    } =>
      Schedule(Person.fromJson(doctor), day, [for (final s in slots) ScheduleSlot.fromJson(s)], info),
    _ => _unexpected('Schedule', json),
  };
}

// an appointment of GET /api/my-area
class Appointment {
  final int id;
  final String day;
  final Slot slot;
  final Person doctor;

  const Appointment(this.id, this.day, this.slot, this.doctor);

  factory Appointment.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'id': final int id, 'day': final String day, 'slot': final Object slot, 'doctor': final Object doctor} =>
      Appointment(id, day, Slot.fromJson(slot), Person.fromJson(doctor)),
    _ => _unexpected('Appointment', json),
  };
}

// GET /api/my-area
class MyArea {
  final Identity patient;
  final List<Appointment> appointments;

  const MyArea(this.patient, this.appointments);

  factory MyArea.fromJson(Object? json) => switch (json) {
    {'patient': final Object patient, 'appointments': final List<Object?> a} => MyArea(Identity.fromJson(patient), [
      for (final r in a) Appointment.fromJson(r),
    ]),
    _ => _unexpected('Area', json),
  };
}

// GET /api/my-account
class MyAccount extends Identity {
  final String login;
  final int version;

  const MyAccount(super.title, super.firstName, super.lastName, this.login, this.version);

  factory MyAccount.fromJson(Object? json) {
    final i = Identity.fromJson(json);
    return switch (json) {
      {'login': final String login, 'version': final int version} => MyAccount(
        i.title,
        i.firstName,
        i.lastName,
        login,
        version,
      ),
      _ => _unexpected('Account', json),
    };
  }
}

The JSON objects of the API, in [Dart] classes (see Example 24):

  • line 14: a function that never terminates normally (it throws an exception): its return type is [Never]. It can therefore serve as the final case for a [switch] of any type;
  • lines 24–30: filtering a [Map]: this case applies if the JSON has (at least) these three keys, with values of these types, which are stored in variables along the way;
  • lines 69–88: a doctor or a client: an [Identity], plus an identifier, a version (the optimistic lock: it is sent back with a modification), and a login, which only the ADMIN receives (hence the optional parameter in square brackets);
  • Lines 109–114: An entry in the calendar, showing the RIGHTS of the logged-in user, calculated by the server: [patient] is only shown to those who have permission to view it, [bookable] indicates whether the user can make a reservation; [appointmentId] is only provided to those who can cancel;
  • lines 129–151: first, the time slot itself ([Slot.fromJson]) is read, followed by its specific fields;
  • lines 209–213: the logged-in patient’s account: their identity, login, and version. [super.title]: the parameter is passed as-is to the parent class constructor.

docs.title: 11.7.5. lib/api/rdvmedecins_api.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/api/rdvmedecins_api.dart - one method per route of the API
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The "data access layer" of the client (a "repository", in the
// vocabulary of Flutter's architecture guide): the screens call
// these typed methods, knowing nothing about the URLs, the http package or the
// JSON. If the API changes, only this file changes.
// Each method returns a Future; on failure, it completes with an
// ApiError (see api_client.dart).
// The data sent (forms) are plain Map<String, Object?>:
// their keys are the names of the fields expected by the server - and those
// of the errors it sends back (ApiError.fields).
// =========================================================================

import 'api_client.dart';
import 'types.dart';

// /api/doctors or /api/clients: both are handled the same way
enum PersonType { doctors, clients }

typedef Data = Map<String, Object?>;

class RdvMedecinsApi {
  final ApiClient _client;

  RdvMedecinsApi(this._client);

  Future<Object?> _get(String url, {bool isPublic = false}) => _client.request('GET', url, isPublic: isPublic);
  Future<Object?> _post(String url, Object body, {bool isPublic = false}) =>
      _client.request('POST', url, body: body, isPublic: isPublic);

  // ------------------------------------------------ login (public routes)
  Future<Captcha> captcha() async => Captcha.fromJson(await _get('/captcha', isPublic: true));

  Future<User> me() async => User.fromJson(await _get('/auth/me', isPublic: true));

  Future<User> logIn(String login, String password, String captchaId, String captcha) async =>
      User.fromJson(
        await _post('/auth/login', {
          'login': login,
          'password': password,
          'captchaId': captchaId,
          'captcha': captcha,
        }, isPublic: true),
      );

  Future<void> logOut() => _post('/auth/logout', {}, isPublic: true);

  // ------------------------------------------------ account creation (public)
  Future<void> registrationAccess(String captchaId, String captcha) =>
      _post('/register/access', {'captchaId': captchaId, 'captcha': captcha}, isPublic: true);

  Future<bool> registrationAccessStatus() async => switch (await _get('/register/access', isPublic: true)) {
    {'valid': true} => true,
    _ => false,
  };

  Future<String> register(Data data) async => switch (await _post('/register', data, isPublic: true)) {
    {'login': final String login} => login,
    final other => throw FormatException('Unexpected response: $other'),
  };

  // ------------------------------------------------ schedule and appointments
  // doctorId null: for a logged-in doctor, THEIR schedule
  Future<Schedule> schedule(int? doctorId, String day) async {
    final params = Uri(queryParameters: {'day': day, 'doctorId': ?doctorId?.toString()}).query;
    return Schedule.fromJson(await _get('/schedule?$params'));
  }

  Future<void> book(String day, int slotId, int? clientId) =>
      _post('/appointments', {'day': day, 'slotId': slotId, 'clientId': ?clientId});

  Future<void> cancelAppointment(int appointmentId) => _client.request('DELETE', '/appointments/$appointmentId');

  // ------------------------------------------------ doctors and clients
  Future<List<Person>> list(PersonType type) async => Person.list(await _get('/${type.name}'));

  Future<Person> read(PersonType type, int id) async => Person.fromJson(await _get('/${type.name}/$id'));

  Future<Person> add(PersonType type, Data data) async =>
      Person.fromJson(await _post('/${type.name}', data));

  Future<Person> edit(PersonType type, int id, Data data) async =>
      Person.fromJson(await _client.request('PUT', '/${type.name}/$id', body: data));

  Future<void> remove(PersonType type, int id) => _client.request('DELETE', '/${type.name}/$id');

  // ------------------------------------------------ the patient's area
  Future<MyArea> myArea() async => MyArea.fromJson(await _get('/my-area'));

  Future<MyAccount> myAccount() async => MyAccount.fromJson(await _get('/my-account'));

  Future<User> editMyAccount(Data data) async =>
      User.fromJson(await _client.request('PUT', '/my-account', body: data));

  Future<void> deleteMyAccount(String currentPassword) =>
      _client.request('DELETE', '/my-account', body: {'currentPassword': currentPassword});
}

One method per API route: this is the [RdvMedecins] class from Example 24, expanded.

  • Line 19: [/api/doctors] and [/api/clients] are handled the same way: an enumeration, where the name of each value ([PersonType.doctors.name], “doctors”) is that of the route;
  • Line 21: A type alias: a more descriptive name for an existing type;
  • lines 33–47: the connection routes, which are public: a 401 has its own specific meaning (“no one is logged in,” “incorrect password”) and does not mean that the session has expired;
  • line 53: Is the account creation token valid? A [switch] expression in the response: [true] only for [{"valid": true}];
  • Lines 65–67: The address parameters, constructed by [Uri] (which encodes them). ['doctorId': ?doctorId?.toString()]: an optional element of [Map] ([Dart] 3.8): the key is added only if the value is not [null]. A logged-in doctor requests the calendar without [doctorId]: the server returns the doctor’s own calendar;
  • line 71: similarly, [clientId] is sent only if it is known (a patient is making a reservation for themselves);
  • lines 76–86: the five operations involving doctors or clients: [/api/${type.name}];
  • lines 89–97: the patient’s area. Deleting the account sends a message body with a [DELETE] request (the current password): this is permitted by HTTP, and the [http] package also allows it, via a manually constructed [http.Request] (see [api_client.dart]).

docs.title: 11.8.1. lib/i18n/translations.dart
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/i18n/translations.dart - the dictionaries, the current language
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Taken from example 21. The dictionaries (assets/i18n/fr.json, en.json)
// are those of the Vue.js, Angular and React clients: same keys, same
// conventions ({{param}}, plurals _one / _other). The server only sends back
// KEYS ("ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN"): it is here that they become
// text, in the language chosen by the user.
//   - t('KEY', {'param': value}) : the text of the current language;
//   - changeLanguage('fr')       : loads the other dictionary, notifies
//                                  the screens (ChangeNotifier), stores
//                                  the choice on the device.
// =========================================================================

import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:flutter/services.dart';
import 'package:flutter/widgets.dart';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

const languages = ['fr', 'en'];

class Translations extends ChangeNotifier {
  final SharedPreferences? _storage;
  String _language = 'en';
  Map<String, Object?> _dictionary = {};

  Translations([this._storage]);

  String get language => _language;

  // the initial language: the one stored on the device, otherwise the one of the
  // phone (if it is known), otherwise English
  Future<void> start() async {
    final stored = _storage?.getString('rdvmedecins.language');
    final device = WidgetsBinding.instance.platformDispatcher.locale.languageCode;
    await changeLanguage(stored ?? (languages.contains(device) ? device : 'en'));
  }

  Future<void> changeLanguage(String language) async {
    // rootBundle: the files shipped with the application (assets section of the pubspec)
    final json = await rootBundle.loadString('assets/i18n/$language.json');
    _dictionary = jsonDecode(json) as Map<String, Object?>;
    _language = language;
    await _storage?.setString('rdvmedecins.language', language);
    notifyListeners();
  }

  // "HOME.HELLO" -> dictionary['HOME']['HELLO']; null if missing
  String? _find(String key) {
    Object? node = _dictionary;
    for (final part in key.split('.')) {
      node = node is Map<String, Object?> ? node[part] : null;
    }
    return node is String ? node : null;
  }

  String t(String key, [Map<String, Object?> params = const {}]) {
    String? text;
    final count = params['count'];
    if (count is int) {
      // Intl.pluralLogic: the plural form, according to the rules of the language
      text = Intl.pluralLogic(
        count,
        locale: _language,
        zero: _find('${key}_zero'),
        one: _find('${key}_one'),
        other: _find('${key}_other'),
      );
    }
    text ??= _find(key);
    // an unknown key is displayed as is: we immediately see what is missing
    if (text == null) return key;
    // {{name}} -> the value of the parameter name
    return text.replaceAllMapped(RegExp(r'\{\{(\w+)\}\}'), (m) => '${params[m[1]] ?? m[0]}');
  }
}

The [Translations] class from Example 21, simplified: the dictionaries always have the same name ([assets/i18n/fr.json]).

  • lines 35–38: the initial language: the one selected during a previous use, otherwise the phone’s language if the app knows it, otherwise English. [platformDispatcher.locale]: the system language;
  • lines 59–76: the translation of a key, including plurals ([_zero], [_one], [_other]) and parameters ([{{name}}]), according to the conventions of [i18next], which are the same as those used in the dictionaries of other clients.
