docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// lib/ex25_server_errors/main.dart - displaying the errors of the SERVER
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The management of the clients (admin account). This form performs,
// DELIBERATELY, no validation on the phone: everything is sent to the
// server, which answers, in case of refusal, with a JSON error (converted into an
// ApiError by common/api.dart):
//
//   400 { key: 'ERRORS.INVALID_FORM', fields: { lastName: 'ERRORS.LASTNAME_REQUIRED' } }
//   409 { key: 'ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS', fields: { firstName: ..., lastName: ... } }
//   409 { key: 'ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE' }         (optimistic lock)
//
// The error of EACH field (ApiError.fields) is stored in the state and
// displayed below the field (errorText); its message is the KEY sent by
// the server, which the screen translates (dictionaries of example 21).
// Modifying a field clears its error.
// Try: an empty last name, a "Dr" title, a namesake (Alice DURAND), a
// login already taken (martin), the same record modified on two devices...
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

import '../common/api.dart';
import '../common/login_bar.dart';
import '../common/http_client.dart';
import '../common/api_error.dart';
import '../common/types.dart';
import '../ex16_confirmation/confirmation.dart';
import '../ex21_i18n/translations.dart';
import '../ex23_login/command.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  final storage = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  final translations = Translations('ex25', storage);
  await translations.start();
  runApp(
    MultiProvider(
      providers: [
        Provider.value(value: Api(CookieClient(storage))),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: translations),
      ],
      child: MaterialApp(
        debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
        theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
        home: const ClientsPage(),
      ),
    ),
  );
}

// the fields of the form
enum Field { title, firstName, lastName, login, password }

class ClientsPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const ClientsPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<ClientsPage> createState() => _ClientsPageState();
}

class _ClientsPageState extends State<ClientsPage> {
  late final Api _api = context.read<Api>();
  User? _user;
  List<Person> _clients = [];

  // the form: _editedId == null -> creation, otherwise update
  int? _editedId;
  int _version = 0;
  String _title = 'Mr';
  final _texts = {
    for (final c in [Field.firstName, Field.lastName, Field.login, Field.password]) c: TextEditingController(),
  };
  // the error of each field (a translation KEY), returned by the server
  Map<String, String> _errors = {};
  // the general message of the last error, and the one of a success (key + parameters)
  ApiError? _pageError;
  ({String key, Map<String, String> params})? _success;
  // sending to the server: a Command (example 23), which tells whether it is in progress
  final _sending = Command();

  bool get _isAdmin => _user?.role == Role.admin;

  @override
  void dispose() {
    for (final c in _texts.values) {
      c.dispose();
    }
    _sending.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  Future<void> _reload() async {
    final clients = Person.list(await _api.get('/clients'));
    if (mounted) setState(() => _clients = clients);
  }

  Future<void> _onUserChange(User? u) async {
    setState(() {
      _user = u;
      _clients = [];
    });
    if (u?.role == Role.admin) await _reload();
  }

  void _clearMessages() {
    _errors = {};
    _pageError = null;
    _success = null;
  }

  void _newForm() {
    setState(() {
      _editedId = null;
      _version = 0;
      _title = 'Mr';
      for (final c in _texts.values) {
        c.clear();
      }
      _clearMessages();
    });
  }

  void _edit(Person c) {
    setState(() {
      _editedId = c.id;
      // the VERSION read with the record goes back with the update: if someone
      // modified the record meanwhile, the server will answer 409 CONCURRENT_UPDATE
      _version = c.version;
      _title = c.title;
      _texts[Field.firstName]!.text = c.firstName;
      _texts[Field.lastName]!.text = c.lastName;
      _texts[Field.login]!.text = c.login ?? '';
      _texts[Field.password]!.clear();
      _clearMessages();
    });
  }

  Future<void> _save() async {
    setState(_clearMessages);
    final input = {
      'title': _title,
      for (final MapEntry(key: field, value: c) in _texts.entries) field.name: c.text,
      'version': _version,
    };
    try {
      final client = Person.fromJson(
        _editedId == null ? await _api.post('/clients', input) : await _api.put('/clients/$_editedId', input),
      );
      final key = _editedId == null ? 'FORM.ADDED' : 'FORM.UPDATED';
      _newForm(); // form cleared, messages cleared...
      // ... except this one
      setState(
        () => _success = (key: key, params: {'name': '${client.firstName} ${client.lastName}', 'login': client.login ?? ''}),
      );
      await _reload();
    } on ApiError catch (e) {
      setState(() {
        _pageError = e; // the general message
        _errors = e.fields; // the error of each field
      });
    }
  }

  Future<void> _delete(Person c) async {
    final t = context.read<Translations>().t;
    final name = '${c.firstName} ${c.lastName}';
    final yes = await confirm(context, t('FORM.DELETE_CONFIRM', {'name': name}));
    if (!yes || !mounted) return;
    setState(_clearMessages);
    try {
      await _api.delete('/clients/${c.id}');
      setState(() => _success = (key: 'FORM.DELETED', params: {'name': name}));
    } on ApiError catch (e) {
      setState(() => _pageError = e);
    }
    await _reload();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final translations = context.watch<Translations>();
    final t = translations.t;

    // an input field, with its error (a key of the server) translated
    Widget field(Field c, {bool secret = false}) => TextField(
      controller: _texts[c],
      obscureText: secret,
      decoration: InputDecoration(
        labelText: t('FORM.${c.name.toUpperCase()}'),
        errorText: _errors[c.name] == null ? null : t(_errors[c.name]!),
        errorMaxLines: 2,
      ),
      // a modified field: its error disappears
      onChanged: (_) {
        if (_errors.containsKey(c.name)) setState(() => _errors = {..._errors}..remove(c.name));
      },
    );

    final success = _success;
    final pageError = _pageError;
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: Text(t('FORM.PAGE_TITLE')),
        actions: [
          // the language: a menu
          PopupMenuButton<String>(
            icon: const Icon(Icons.translate),
            onSelected: translations.changeLanguage,
            itemBuilder: (_) => [for (final l in languages) PopupMenuItem(value: l, child: Text(l.toUpperCase()))],
          ),
        ],
      ),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
        children: [
          LoginBar(onUserChange: _onUserChange),
          if (_user != null && !_isAdmin)
            Card(
              color: Colors.amber.shade50,
              child: Padding(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12), child: Text(t('FORM.ADMIN_ONLY'))),
            ),
          if (_isAdmin) ...[
            for (final c in _clients)
              ListTile(
                dense: true,
                title: Text(c.fullName),
                subtitle: Text(c.login ?? ''),
                trailing: Row(
                  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
                  children: [
                    IconButton(tooltip: t('FORM.EDIT'), icon: const Icon(Icons.edit), onPressed: () => _edit(c)),
                    IconButton(
                      tooltip: t('FORM.DELETE'),
                      icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline, color: Colors.red),
                      onPressed: () => _delete(c),
                    ),
                  ],
                ),
              ),
            Card(
              child: Padding(
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
                child: Column(
                  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                  children: [
                    Text(
                      t(_editedId == null ? 'FORM.TITLE_ADD' : 'FORM.TITLE_EDIT'),
                      style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium,
                    ),
                    // a "Dr" title that the server will refuse: to see ERRORS.INVALID_TITLE
                    DropdownButton<String>(
                      value: _title,
                      items: [
                        for (final title in ['Mr', 'Mme', 'Melle', 'Dr'])
                          DropdownMenuItem(value: title, child: Text(title)),
                      ],
                      onChanged: (v) => setState(() {
                        _title = v!;
                        _errors = {..._errors}..remove('title');
                      }),
                    ),
                    if (_errors['title'] != null)
                      Text(t(_errors['title']!), style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.red, fontSize: 12)),
                    field(Field.firstName),
                    field(Field.lastName),
                    field(Field.login),
                    field(Field.password, secret: true),
                    const SizedBox(height: 12),
                    ListenableBuilder(
                      listenable: _sending,
                      builder: (context, _) => Wrap(
                        spacing: 8,
                        children: [
                          FilledButton(
                            onPressed: _sending.running ? null : () => _sending.execute(_save),
                            child: Text(t('FORM.SAVE')),
                          ),
                          OutlinedButton(onPressed: _newForm, child: Text(t('FORM.CANCEL'))),
                        ],
                      ),
                    ),
                    if (success != null)
                      Padding(
                        padding: const EdgeInsets.only(top: 12),
                        child: Text(t(success.key, success.params), style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.green)),
                      ),
                    // the general message, and the HTTP status, to understand
                    if (pageError != null)
                      Padding(
                        padding: const EdgeInsets.only(top: 12),
                        child: Text.rich(
                          TextSpan(
                            children: [
                              TextSpan(
                                text: t(pageError.key, pageError.params),
                                style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.red),
                              ),
                              TextSpan(
                                text: '  ($pageError)',
                                style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.grey, fontSize: 12),
                              ),
                            ],
                          ),
                        ),
                      ),
                  ],
                ),
              ),
            ),
          ],
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}

Patient management (admin account). This form does not perform any validation on the phone: everything is sent to the server, which responds—in case of rejection—with an error JSON, converted to [ApiError].

  • Lines 37–43: the translations from Example 21, using the dictionaries from that example;
  • line 77: the error for each field: a translation KEY, returned by the server;
  • lines 79–82: the general message for the last error, the success message, and the [Command] sent to the server (Example 23);
  • lines 126–131: the version read from the record is updated with the change: if someone has modified the record in the meantime, the server will respond with a 409 [CONCURRENT_UPDATE] (optimistic lock);
  • lines 141–162: the save operation: [POST /api/clients] (creation) or [PUT /api/clients/:id] (update). If the operation is rejected, [ApiError] returns a general error message and the specific error for each field;
  • lines 188–198: an input field: its error, a server key, is translated and displayed below the field ([errorText]); editing the field clears its error;
  • lines 209–212: a menu in the top bar for language selection;
  • line 257: a “Dr” title, which the server will reject: see [ERRORS.INVALID_TITLE];
  • lines 291–302: the general message, translated, and, for context, the status HTTP and the key.

An empty form; a homonym (“Alice DURAND”); the same, in French:

Also try: a username that’s already taken ([martin]), an invalid username (“Jean M”), and the same record edited on two devices (or in the app and with [curl]).

The principle is the same as for all forms in the case study: the rules reside in ONE place—the server; the app displays the results in the user’s language.

docs.title: 13. Conclusion
docs.text:
We have developed the [Flutter] client for the [RdvMedecins] application. For the user, it offers the same screens as the HTML application from the [NestJS] course and as the [Vue.js], [Angular] and [React] from previous courses; however, this is a mobile app installed on the phone, and the same code also generates a web app.

The server, on the other hand, hasn’t changed. Its API and JSON—whose contract (routes, body, codes, and error keys) was sufficient to write the client without ever reading its code—serves both a browser and a phone equally well. There is only one difference: on the phone, there is no browser to store the token cookie, so the app took on that role with just a few lines of code ([CookieClient]). Security remains unchanged: it is still the server that authenticates users, verifies roles and management rules, and decides what a patient is authorized to view.

Readers who have taken the [React] course can compare:

  • both are based on the same idea: the interface is a function of the state. A [React] component is a function that returns JSX; a [Flutter] widget has a [build()] method that returns a widget tree. When the state changes ([useState] / [setState]), the interface is rebuilt and then compared to the previous one;
  • [React] generates HTML, which the browser renders; [Flutter] renders each pixel itself, using its own engine, on both the phone and in the browser. This results in identical screens across all platforms, but a web application that takes longer to load;
  • [Flutter] provides much more than [React]: the widgets from [Material], forms, lists, windows, animations, the theme, and tests. Fewer libraries were required: [go_router] for addresses, [provider] for shared state, and [http] for queries. No CSS: the layout is built using widgets ([Column], [Row], [Padding], [Expanded]...);
  • [Dart] is a typed, compiled language with non-nullable types: many errors that [TypeScript] overlooks (a missing [null] value, a misread JSON) are detected at compile time, or as soon as the response is received thanks to [Dart] 3 filtering;
  • the trade-off: more verbose screens (the widget tree is deep), and a lifecycle to be familiar with ([initState], [didUpdateWidget], [dispose], [mounted]).

Concepts covered in this course (stateless and stateful widgets, lifecycle, keys, [InheritedWidget] and [provider], [ChangeNotifier], [Future], and [Stream], router and guards, forms, internationalization) are common to any [Flutter] application. For further reading:

  • the official documentation, docs.flutter.dev, its tutorials, and its architecture guide (“App architecture”);
  • tests: widget tests ([flutter_test]), which interact with a screen without a phone (the screenshots in this document were created using these tests), and integration tests ([integration_test]), which run the actual application on an emulator;
  • other widely used state managers: [Riverpod] (the successor to [provider], by the same author), [Bloc];
  • Code generation: [json_serializable] and [freezed] generate the methods [fromJson], [copyWith], [==]... from simple declarations;
  • secure token storage ([flutter_secure_storage]), notifications, the camera, geolocation: one package per need, on pub.dev;
  • iPhone: the same code generates an application [iOS], to be built on a [Mac] using [Xcode].

docs.title: 12. Deployment
docs.text: During development, the application runs under the control of [flutter run]: in “debug” mode, which is slower, with hot reloading and checks ([assert]) performed by [Flutter]. To deploy it, we build it in “release” mode: optimized code, without development tools. We build one version per platform.

docs.title: 12.1. The web version
docs.text:
1. Build the client. In the [rdvmedecins_flutter] folder:
flutter build web --no-web-resources-cdn

The console displays:

Compiling lib\main.dart for the Web...
Wasm dry run succeeded. Consider building and testing your application with the `--wasm` flag. See docs for more info: https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/web/wasm
Use --no-wasm-dry-run to disable these warnings.
Expected to find fonts for (MaterialIcons, packages/cupertino_icons/CupertinoIcons), but found (MaterialIcons). This usually means you are referring to font families in an IconData class but not including them in the assets section of your pubspec.yaml, are missing the package that would include them, or are missing "uses-material-design: true".
Font asset "MaterialIcons-Regular.otf" was tree-shaken, reducing it from 1645184 to 9004 bytes (99.5% reduction). Tree-shaking can be disabled by providing the --no-tree-shake-icons flag when building your app.
Compiling lib\main.dart for the Web...                             70,5s
√ Built build\web

Two warnings, with no consequences: compilation into [WebAssembly] would be possible (see below); a library in [Flutter] references icons from the [iOS] ([CupertinoIcons]) style, which the application does not use.

The [dart2js] compiler has compiled the entire application ([Dart], [Flutter], and the packages) into [JavaScript], in the [build/web/] folder:

  • [index.html]: THE application page, which loads [flutter_bootstrap.js], then [main.dart.js] (3.5 MB, approximately 1 MB once compressed by the server): OUR code, along with all the code from [Flutter] and the packages, optimized. [Flutter] does not generate HTML: the application draws each pixel itself on a canvas, using the same engine as on the phone;
  • [canvaskit/]: this rendering engine ([Skia], compiled into [WebAssembly]: [canvaskit.wasm], 7 MB). Without the [--no-web-resources-cdn] option, it would be downloaded from a [Google] server; with it, it is included with the application, which no longer depends on any external site;
  • [assets/]: the resources from [pubspec.yaml] (dictionaries, fonts). The icons are “tree-shaken”: only those used by the application are kept in the icon font;
  • Upon first load, the browser downloads a few megabytes (primarily the rendering engine) and then caches them. This is the main weakness of [Flutter] for the web: it is better suited for applications (which are opened and used for extended periods) than for websites (which are browsed briefly).

The [--wasm] option compiles the application as [WebAssembly] rather than [JavaScript]: it is faster in browsers that support it (recent versions of [Chrome], [Edge], and [Firefox]); other browsers automatically receive the [JavaScript] version.

  1. Place it on the server. Copy the CONTENTS of the [build/web/] folder to a folder named [client/] at the root of the JSON server ([rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client/index.html], [rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client/main.dart.js]...), then restart the server. It displays:
[Nest] LOG [RdvMedecins] web client served from .../rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client
[Nest] LOG [RdvMedecins] JSON server started: http://localhost:8080/api

The complete application is now available at http://localhost:8080. The server serves the client’s files and returns [index.html] for any other address outside of /api: reloading the /schedule page works (it is the client’s router that displays it). The server’s [src/web/client-spa.ts] file handles this task. The application is served by the API server: the relative address of [config.dart] ([''], or [/api/...]) is correct.

You can also try the version built without the JSON server, using any file server, but the /api requests will fail.

docs.title: 12.2. The Android version
docs.text:
1. Build the app, specifying the server address:
flutter build apk --dart-define=SERVER=http://192.168.1.20:8080

The console displays (for a APK built without [--dart-define]):

Running Gradle task 'assembleRelease'...
Font asset "MaterialIcons-Regular.otf" was tree-shaken, reducing it from 1645184 to 3400 bytes (99.8% reduction). Tree-shaking can be disabled by providing the --no-tree-shake-icons flag when building your app.
Running Gradle task 'assembleRelease'...                          193,4s
√ Built build\app\outputs\flutter-apk\app-release.apk (53.5MB)

(A few warnings regarding [Gradle] and [Java], which had no impact, have been removed.) The first build takes a long time: [Gradle] downloads its own tools and libraries; subsequent builds are much faster.

The [Dart] compiler translated the application into machine code for the three processor families of [Android] phones (ARM 32-bit, ARM 64-bit, x86 64-bit), and the [Android] build tool ([Gradle]) packaged it, along with the [Flutter] engine, into a APK file: the [Android] application installation format. It contains three copies of the application and its engine—one per processor family—which explains its size. [--split-per-abi] would generate three smaller APK files, one per processor family; an “App Bundle” (see below) allows the store to deliver only what each phone needs.

  1. Install it. With the phone connected to the computer (USB cable, USB debugging enabled):
flutter install

You can also copy the APK file to the phone and open it: [Android] will then ask you to allow the installation of apps “from unknown sources.”

  1. For a real release:
  • the app must be signed with a developer-specific key: the project generated by [flutter create] signs the “release” version with the debug key, which is sufficient for testing but not for a store. The [Flutter] documentation (“Build and release an Android app”) describes how to create the key and configure [Gradle];
  • [Google Play Store] expects an “Android App Bundle” rather than a APK: [flutter build appbundle];
  • The app name and icon are configured in [android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml] ([android:label]) and [android/app/src/main/res/mipmap-*/];
  • The server must be set to HTTPS (passwords are shared), and the line [android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"] is removed from the manifest.

docs.title: 12.3. The production server
docs.text:
In actual production, don’t forget the [.env] file on the server:

  • a long, random [JWT_SECRET];
  • an empty [CAPTCHA_TEST];
  • [COOKIE_SECURE=true] if the site is served via HTTPS (it must be). The mobile client sends the cookie regardless of this option: it is the browser that enforces it;
  • [TRUST_PROXY=true] if the server is located behind a proxy ([nginx]...), so that the attempt limit sees the clients’ actual IP address.

We then launch the compiled server: [npm run build], followed by [npm run start:prod].

docs.title: 3.1. Example 01: The Structure of a Flutter Application
3.1.1. The Project
docs.text:
A [Flutter] project is created using the [flutter create] command:

flutter create --org fr.stahe --platforms=android,web,windows my_application
  • [--org fr.stahe]: the prefix of the app ID, reversed like a domain name. The app [Android] will be named [fr.stahe.my_application]; two apps installed on the same phone must have different IDs;
  • [--platforms=...]: the target platforms. For each one, [flutter create] creates a folder ([android/], [web/], [windows/], and also [ios/], [macos/], [linux/] if requested): a small, platform-specific project that simply launches the [Flutter] engine and loads the application into it. We rarely make changes to it (the application’s name, icon, and permissions);
  • [my_application]: the project name, which is also the package name [Dart]: lowercase letters, numbers, and underscores.

The command generates a complete, ready-to-run application (a counter). The example project was created in the same way, and then its [lib/] folder was filled in manually to combine twenty-five applications into a single project: this way, they share the same packages, which are downloaded only once.

docs.title: 3.1.2. The pubspec.yaml file
docs.text:
The [pubspec.yaml] file describes the project: its name, the required version of [Dart], the packages used, and the files included with the application. The one for the examples:

# ==========================================================================
# pubspec.yaml - the description of the examples project
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A single Flutter project for the 25 examples: each one has its folder in
# lib/ and its own entry point (main.dart), given to the command
# flutter run with the -t (target) option:
#
#     flutter run -t lib/ex05_controlled_fields/main.dart
#
# The libraries (the "packages") are downloaded from pub.dev by the
# flutter pub get command (run automatically by flutter run).
# ==========================================================================

name: examples_flutter
description: The 25 small examples of the course Step-by-step introduction to the Flutter framework.
# no publication on pub.dev: this is an application, not a library
publish_to: none
version: 1.0.0

environment:
  # the required version of the Dart language
  sdk: ^3.12.0

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  # "clean" addresses on the web (example 17)
  flutter_web_plugins:
    sdk: flutter
  # the texts of Flutter itself (dialog buttons, calendar...)
  # in English and in French (examples 05, 21)
  flutter_localizations:
    sdk: flutter
  # dates and numbers formatted according to the language (examples 09, 21)
  intl: any
  # the router (examples 17, 18)
  go_router: ^16.2.0
  # a state shared by the whole application (examples 20, 24, 25)
  provider: ^6.1.5
  # a small key -> value dictionary, kept on the device (examples 20, 21, 23)
  shared_preferences: ^2.5.3
  # HTTP requests (examples 22 to 25)
  http: ^1.5.0
  # displaying SVG images (example 03, captcha of examples 22 to 25)
  flutter_svg: ^2.2.1

dev_dependencies:
  # the tests (and the course screenshots, see test/captures)
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
  # the style rules recommended by the Flutter team (see analysis_options.yaml)
  flutter_lints: ^6.0.0

flutter:
  # the Material Design icons (Icons.add, Icons.delete...)
  uses-material-design: true
  # the files shipped WITH the application: they are read by their path
  assets:
    - assets/
    - assets/i18n/
  # a monospaced font (to display JSON), shipped with the application
  fonts:
    - family: RobotoMono
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/RobotoMono-Regular.ttf
        - asset: assets/fonts/RobotoMono-Bold.ttf
          weight: 700
  • Lines 14–18: the project name (which is also the package name—the project files are imported via [package:examples_flutter/...]), its description, and its version. [publish_to: none]: This project is not a library; it will never be published on [pub.dev];
  • lines 20–22: the required version of the [Dart] language. The prefix [^] accepts any newer version within the same major version (3.12, 3.13… but not 4.0);
  • lines 24–45: the packages required by the application. Some come from the [Flutter] SDK itself ([sdk: flutter]): [flutter] (the framework), [flutter_localizations] (the texts from [Flutter] translated into each language), [flutter_web_plugins] (a web-specific configuration). The others are downloaded from pub.dev, the repository for the [Dart] packages: their purpose is explained in the comments, and each will be demonstrated in the example that uses it. [intl: any]: any version ([flutter_localizations] dictates its own);
  • lines 47–52: packages used only for development and not included in the shipped application: [flutter_test] (tests) and [flutter_lints] (parser style rules);
  • lines 54–67: the configuration specific to [Flutter]:
    • [uses-material-design: true]: the application uses the icon font from [Material Design] ([Icons.add], [Icons.delete]...) ;
    • [assets]: the files included with the application (images, dictionaries, etc.), which are read by their path. Specifying a folder ([assets/]) delivers all the files it contains directly;
    • [fonts]: a font included with the application; [Roboto Mono], a monospaced font, is used to display JSON. The standard font for [Material Design], [Roboto], is the system font [Android]: there is no need to include it.

Package versions follow the same convention as [npm]: [^16.2.0] accepts any version of 16.x.y starting from 16.2.0. The command [flutter pub get] downloads the packages and writes the exact selected versions to the file [pubspec.lock]. It is launched automatically by [flutter run] when [pubspec.yaml] has changed; [VS Code] also runs it as soon as this file is saved. To add a package, rather than editing the file manually, you can type [flutter pub add go_router]: the command adds the line with the latest version of the package.

docs.title: 3.1.3. The analysis_options.yaml file
docs.text:
The [Dart] parser checks the code as you type: [VS Code] underlines errors in red and warnings in yellow or blue. You can also run it for the entire project with [flutter analyze]. Its rules:

# ==========================================================================
# analysis_options.yaml - the rules of the Dart code analyzer
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The analyzer checks the code while it is typed (VS Code underlines the
# errors) and through the flutter analyze command. We start from the rules
# recommended by the Flutter team (flutter_lints package)...
# ==========================================================================

include: package:flutter_lints/flutter.yaml

analyzer:
  language:
    # ... made stricter: no implicit conversion of a dynamic type
    strict-casts: true
    strict-raw-types: true

linter:
  rules:
    # single quotes everywhere, as in the course examples
    prefer_single_quotes: true
    # "final" for a local variable that is never reassigned
    prefer_final_locals: true
    # strings that are too long are allowed (texts of the examples)
    lines_longer_than_80_chars: false
  • line 9: the rules recommended by the [Flutter] team ([flutter_lints] package): a widget must have a constructor [const] if possible, a controller must be released, etc.;
  • Lines 14–15: stricter typing. [Dart] is a statically typed language, but it has a type [dynamic] (“anything”): the decoded JSON, for example, is made up of [dynamic]. [strict-casts] prohibits implicit conversion to another type: you must write it explicitly ([json['lastName'] as String]), and any error occurs there and is visible;
  • Lines 20–24: a few style rules: use single quotes for strings (double quotes if the string contains an apostrophe: ["it's"]), and [final] for variables that are never reassigned.

docs.title: 3.1.4. The entry point: main.dart
docs.text:
For example, there is a file named [main.dart], which contains the function [main]—the entry point for any program named [Dart]. The one from Example 01:

// =========================================================================
// lib/ex01_first_application/main.dart - a first application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Everything, in a Flutter application, is a WIDGET: an object that describes
// a piece of the screen (a text, a button, a margin, a column...).
// Widgets are nested inside one another and form a TREE.
// A widget has a build() method, which RETURNS the widgets that
// make it up. Flutter calls build() to produce the screen; it
// CALLS IT AGAIN each time the state of the widget changes (setState), and
// updates the screen with the new result.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

// "ordinary" data, outside the widgets: they never change
const title = 'Welcome to Flutter';
const languages = ['Dart', 'Flutter', 'Material Design'];

// "12:05:09": the current time, on two digits
String currentTime() {
  final d = DateTime.now();
  String twoDigits(int n) => n.toString().padLeft(2, '0');
  return '${twoDigits(d.hour)}:${twoDigits(d.minute)}:${twoDigits(d.second)}';
}

// the entry point of every Dart program
void main() {
  // runApp: Flutter takes over the screen and displays the ROOT widget on it
  runApp(const Application());
}

// the root widget: it configures the application (title, theme, first screen).
// StatelessWidget: a widget WITHOUT state, entirely described by its parameters
class Application extends StatelessWidget {
  const Application({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // MaterialApp: an application with the colors and the behavior of
    // Material Design, Google's visual language
    return MaterialApp(
      title: 'Example 01',
      // no "DEBUG" banner in the corner of the screen
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      // the colors of the whole application, derived from a base color
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      home: const HomePage(),
    );
  }
}

// a widget WITH state: it comes in two parts, the widget itself (which never
// changes) and a State object (which holds the data that change)
class HomePage extends StatefulWidget {
  const HomePage({super.key});

  @override
  State<HomePage> createState() => _HomePageState();
}

// the "_": this class is PRIVATE, invisible outside this file
class _HomePageState extends State<HomePage> {
  // the STATE: simple fields of the State object
  int _counter = 0;
  String _time = currentTime();

  // the function called by the button
  void _increment() {
    // setState: the state is modified INSIDE the function passed to setState;
    // Flutter then calls build() again to update the screen. We never
    // modify the screen ourselves
    setState(() {
      _counter++;
      _time = currentTime();
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // Scaffold: the structure of a Material screen (top bar, body...)
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Example 01 - a first application')),
      // Padding: a margin around its child
      body: Padding(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        // Column: children placed one below the other
        child: Column(
          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
          children: [
            Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall),
            const SizedBox(height: 12),
            const Text(
              'This screen is produced by Flutter, from the main function '
              'and the Application and HomePage widgets.',
            ),
            const SizedBox(height: 8),
            // ${expression} inserts the value of an expression into a string
            Text('It is written in ${languages.join(', ')} (${languages.length} languages).'),
            const SizedBox(height: 16),
            // onPressed: the function to call when the button is pressed (see example 04)
            FilledButton(onPressed: _increment, child: const Text('Click me')),
            const SizedBox(height: 16),
            Text(
              'You clicked $_counter times (last click: $_time).',
              style: const TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold, color: Color(0xFF087EA4)),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Let’s start at the end: the program.

  • Line 13: the [Material] library from [Flutter]: all the widgets from [Material Design], the visual language of [Google] (buttons, input fields, bars, windows, etc.). It imports the rest of [Flutter] itself;
  • lines 16–17: two ordinary data values, declared outside the widgets: they never change. [const]: a constant known at compile time;
  • lines 20–23: an ordinary function that returns the current time in the format “12:05:09.” It contains a small function of its own, [twoDigits], written on a single line with [=>];
  • lines 27–29: the function [main], called at launch. [runApp] starts [Flutter]: it takes control of the screen and displays the widget provided to it—the root of the application.

The root widget, [Application]:

  • Line 34: A widget is a class. This class inherits from [StatelessWidget], a stateless widget: what it displays depends solely on its parameters and never changes on its own;
  • Line 29: its constructor. [{super.key}]: an optional named parameter passed to the parent class. Every widget has one: the “key” that identifies it (see Example 04). The constructor is [const]: [Application()] can be a constant that [Flutter] never needs to reconstruct;
  • Lines 38–47: the [build] method, the core of a widget. It returns the widgets that make it up. [@override]: it overrides the [build] method of the parent class. The parameter [context] is the widget’s position in the widget tree: it is used to retrieve what its ancestors provide (the theme, for example, line 90);
  • lines 41–47: [MaterialApp] is the widget that turns a widget tree into an application [Material]: a title ([title], the application’s name in the phone’s recent apps list or the browser tab), a theme ([theme]), and a home screen ([home]). [debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false] removes the “DEBUG” banner that a development app displays in a corner. [ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo)]: All colors in the application (buttons, bars, fields, etc.) are derived from a single base color, according to the rules in [Material Design] 3.

The first screen, [HomePage], has data that changes: it is a stateful widget.

  • Lines 54–58: A [StatefulWidget] consists of two parts. The widget itself, like any widget, never changes (its fields would be [final]); its sole task is to create, via [createState], a [State] object, which in turn contains the data that changes. [Flutter] creates this object once and retains it as long as the widget remains in the same place in the tree;
  • line 62: the object [State]. Its name begins with an underscore: in [Dart], everything beginning with [_] is private and invisible outside the file;
  • lines 64–65: the state: simple fields of the [State] object;
  • lines 68–75: the method called by the button. It does not affect the screen: it changes the state within the function passed to [setState]. [setState] executes this function, then notifies [Flutter] that the state has changed: [Flutter] will call [build], compare the new widget tree to the old one, and redraw what has changed;
  • lines 79–105: the [build] for the screen:
    • [Scaffold] (“scaffolding”) is the structure of a screen [Material]: a top bar ([appBar]), a body ([body]), and, if requested, a bottom bar, a floating button, and a side menu;
    • [AppBar]: the top bar; its title is a widget ([Text]), as is almost everything in [Flutter];
    • [Padding]: a margin around its single child, [child]. [EdgeInsets.all(16)]: 16 points on each side (a logical “point,” independent of screen density: approximately 2.6 pixels on the phone shown in the screenshots);
    • [Column]: its children, [children], arranged one below the other. [crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start]: left-aligned (the “transverse” axis of a column is the horizontal axis);
    • [Text]: text. Its style may be derived from the theme: [Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall] is the style for “small headings”;
    • [SizedBox]: an empty box with a specified height—a space between two widgets;
    • line 98: [${expression}] inserts the value of an expression into a string; [$_counter] is sufficient for a simple variable (line 104);
    • line 101: a button. [onPressed] takes the function to be called when the button is pressed. We specify the function itself, without parentheses: [onPressed: _increment()] would call it immediately, during screen construction;
    • lines 104–105: text that depends on the state. When the state changes, [build] is called, and this text changes.

Two notes regarding [Dart]:

  • almost all widget arguments are named parameters ([title: ...], [child: ...]): the widget tree reads like a description, and the order of the arguments does not matter. A named parameter is optional, unless it is declared as [required];
  • the keyword [const] preceding a widget ([const SizedBox(height: 12)]) creates it once and for all at compile time. [Flutter] then knows that it never changes and doesn’t waste time comparing it. The parser flags any [const] that have been omitted; [VS Code] knows how to add them on its own.

The screen’s widget tree, as shown by the [Flutter DevTools] tool (widget inspector):

Application
└── MaterialApp
    └── HomePage
        └── Scaffold
            ├── AppBar
            │   └── Text
            └── Padding
                └── Column
                    ├── Text          (the title)
                    ├── SizedBox
                    ├── Text
                    ├── SizedBox
                    ├── Text
                    ├── SizedBox
                    ├── FilledButton
                    │   └── Text
                    ├── SizedBox
                    └── Text          (the counter)

In a [Flutter] application, you write very little “implementation” code and a lot of “descriptive” code: the screen is a tree of widgets, each configured by its parameters. This is the same concept as JSX from [React], but without a template language: the tree is written in [Dart].

docs.text:
In the console open to the [examples_flutter] folder, with the [Android] emulator running:

The first time, building the [Android] application (using the [Gradle] tool) takes one or two minutes; subsequent builds take just a few seconds. The application installs on the emulator and starts. On the left, the startup screen; on the right, after pressing the button twice:

Two experiments to try:

  • Change the title text in [main.dart], save the file, and type `r` in the console (or simply save the file in [VS Code]): the screen updates in one second, and the counter retains its value. This is a “hot reload”: the new code is injected into the running application; [Flutter] calls [build], but the [State] objects are preserved. R (“hot restart”) restarts the application from [main]: the counter resets to 0;
  • Launch the same application in the browser: [flutter run -d chrome -t lib/ex01_first_application/main.dart]. It is the same screen, rendered by the same engine; only the window size changes. With [-d windows], it is an application [Windows].

docs.title: 3.2. Example 02: The state and calculated values
docs.text:
The status is the core of [Flutter], just as it is for [React]. This example calculates the price including VAT of an item:

// =========================================================================
// lib/ex02_state/main.dart - the state and the computed values
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A small calculator of prices including VAT:
//   - the STATE: the fields of the State object; changing them INSIDE setState()
//     makes build() run again, which produces the screen with the new values;
//   - a value COMPUTED from the state is NOT state: it is a
//     "getter" (or a local variable of build), recomputed on each call
//     of build(). It is always up to date, with nothing to synchronize;
//   - a piece of data that depends on the SUCCESSIVE values of the state (the history
//     of the totals) is updated where the state changes: in setState;
//   - the title of the application (browser tab, list of the
//     phone's recent applications) is a widget too, Title:
//     it follows the state like the rest of the screen.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

// a formatter of amounts in euros, the American way (€1,234.50), see example 09
final euros = NumberFormat.currency(locale: 'en_US', symbol: '€');

void main() {
  runApp(
    MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      home: const CalculatorPage(),
    ),
  );
}

class CalculatorPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const CalculatorPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<CalculatorPage> createState() => _CalculatorPageState();
}

class _CalculatorPageState extends State<CalculatorPage> {
  // the state
  String _label = 'Pen';
  double _priceExclVat = 2.5;
  int _quantity = 1;
  double _vatRate = 20; // in %
  // the history of the last 5 changes of the total including VAT
  final List<String> _history = [];

  // a controller gives access to the TEXT of an input field: we need one
  // here to put it back to its initial value (Reset). Example 05
  // studies them in detail
  final _labelField = TextEditingController(text: 'Pen');
  final _priceField = TextEditingController(text: '2.5');

  // COMPUTED values: getters, recomputed on each read
  double get _totalExclVat => _quantity * _priceExclVat;
  double get _vatAmount => _totalExclVat * _vatRate / 100;
  double get _totalInclVat => _totalExclVat + _vatAmount;

  // ALL the changes of the state go through this method: it notes the
  // total including VAT before the change, applies the change, and completes
  // the history if the total has changed
  void _change(void Function() change) {
    final oldTotal = _totalInclVat;
    setState(() {
      change();
      if (_totalInclVat != oldTotal) {
        _history.insert(0, '${euros.format(oldTotal)} -> ${euros.format(_totalInclVat)}');
        if (_history.length > 5) {
          _history.removeLast();
        }
      }
    });
  }

  // changing the item resets the quantity to 1: we do it where we know
  // WHY the state changes
  void _changeLabel(String newValue) {
    _change(() {
      _label = newValue;
      _quantity = 1;
    });
  }

  void _reset() {
    _change(() {
      _label = 'Pen';
      _priceExclVat = 2.5;
      _quantity = 1;
      _vatRate = 20;
    });
    _labelField.text = 'Pen';
    _priceField.text = '2.5';
  }

  // the State object disappears (we leave the screen): the controllers are released
  @override
  void dispose() {
    _labelField.dispose();
    _priceField.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final totalStyle = Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleMedium!.copyWith(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold);

    // Title: the title of the application FOLLOWS the state, like everything else
    return Title(
      title: 'Incl. VAT: ${euros.format(_totalInclVat)}',
      color: Colors.indigo,
      child: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Example 02 - the state')),
        // ListView: a column that scrolls if it exceeds the height of the screen
        body: ListView(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          children: [
            Card(
              child: Padding(
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
                child: Column(
                  children: [
                    // onChanged: called on each keystroke, with the new text
                    TextField(
                      controller: _labelField,
                      decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Item'),
                      onChanged: _changeLabel,
                    ),
                    TextField(
                      controller: _priceField,
                      decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Unit price excl. VAT'),
                      // the numeric keyboard of the phone, with the decimal point
                      keyboardType: const TextInputType.numberWithOptions(decimal: true),
                      // tryParse: null if the text is not a number; a comma is accepted too
                      onChanged: (text) => _change(() => _priceExclVat = double.tryParse(text.replaceAll(',', '.')) ?? 0),
                    ),
                    const SizedBox(height: 12),
                    Row(
                      children: [
                        const Expanded(child: Text('Quantity (back to 1 if the item changes)')),
                        IconButton(
                          icon: const Icon(Icons.remove),
                          // null: the button is disabled
                          onPressed: _quantity > 0 ? () => _change(() => _quantity--) : null,
                        ),
                        Text('$_quantity', style: totalStyle),
                        IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.add), onPressed: () => _change(() => _quantity++)),
                      ],
                    ),
                    const SizedBox(height: 8),
                    // buttons of which only ONE is selected: the VAT rate
                    SegmentedButton<double>(
                      segments: const [
                        ButtonSegment(value: 5.5, label: Text('5.5%')),
                        ButtonSegment(value: 10, label: Text('10%')),
                        ButtonSegment(value: 20, label: Text('20%')),
                      ],
                      selected: {_vatRate},
                      onSelectionChanged: (choice) => _change(() => _vatRate = choice.first),
                    ),
                    const SizedBox(height: 12),
                    OutlinedButton(onPressed: _reset, child: const Text('Reset')),
                  ],
                ),
              ),
            ),
            Card(
              child: Padding(
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
                child: Column(
                  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                  children: [
                    Text('$_quantity x $_label', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
                    const Divider(),
                    _line('Total excl. VAT', euros.format(_totalExclVat)),
                    _line('VAT ($_vatRate%)', euros.format(_vatAmount)),
                    _line('Total incl. VAT', euros.format(_totalInclVat), style: totalStyle),
                  ],
                ),
              ),
            ),
            Card(
              child: Padding(
                padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
                child: Column(
                  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
                  children: [
                    Text('History of the total incl. VAT', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleSmall),
                    // one line of text per element of the history (see example 03)
                    for (final line in _history) Text('• $line'),
                  ],
                ),
              ),
            ),
          ],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }

  // a "label ....... amount" line: a method that produces widgets
  Widget _line(String label, String amount, {TextStyle? style}) {
    return Padding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(vertical: 4),
      child: Row(
        children: [
          Expanded(child: Text(label, style: style)),
          Text(amount, style: style),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • Line 21: A US English-style amount formatter (€1,234.50), created once and for all outside the widgets, using the [intl] package (see Example 09). [final]: a variable that is assigned only once, but whose value is not known until runtime (unlike [const]);
  • lines 23–28: the program; this time, [MaterialApp] is written directly into [main]. This is how most examples will begin;
  • lines 42–45: four state data items, simple fields, typed as: [String], [double], [int]. In [Dart], [int], and [double], there are two distinct types of numbers;
  • line 47: the history of the last five changes to the total, a list. The field is [final]: the list will never be replaced; it will be modified (additions, removals);
  • Lines 52–53: two input field controllers. An input field [Flutter] stores its text in a controller, which is created and assigned to it: the text can then be read or changed from within the code (Reset button). Example 05 covers these in detail;
  • lines 56–58: three values calculated from the state. These are NOT state fields; they are getters—methods without parentheses that are used like fields ([_totalInclVat]). They are recalculated each time they are read, so they are always up to date. This is the same rule we’ve already seen with [React]: we only store in the state what we cannot calculate; everything else is calculated;
  • Lines 63–73: The history of the totals including VAT depends on successive values of the total, which a getter cannot express. Therefore, ALL state changes go through the [_change] method, which receives the change to be made as a parameter (a function with no parameters or return value, of type [void Function()]): it records the total before the change, applies the change in `[setState]`, compares it with the total after the change, and updates the history if it has changed. This is the natural place for this calculation: where the state changes, and not in `[build]` (which should only describe the screen);
  • lines 78–81: Changing the item resets the quantity to 1. This is done in the method that handles the field change, where we know why the state is changing;
  • lines 85–93: multiple state changes within a single [setState]: [build] will be called only once. Then the controllers receive their initial text: the fields display it immediately;
  • lines 98–101: [dispose] is called when the [State] object disappears permanently (the screen is exited). Here, the created objects—in this case, the controls—are released. Example 13 will illustrate the lifecycle of an object [State].

The [build] method:

  • line 106: a text style, calculated based on the theme—the medium-sized heading style ([titleMedium]), in bold. [copyWith] creates a copy of an object whose properties are modified: this is a convention of [Flutter] that we’ll see often. [!] tells [Dart] that the value is not [null] (the type of [titleMedium] is [TextStyle?], a style, or [null]);
  • Lines 109–111: The [Title] widget provides the application’s title: on the web, this is the browser tab title; on [Android], it is the name displayed in the list of recent applications. Whereas [React] used an effect ([useEffect]) to modify [document.title] after it was displayed, [Flutter] doesn’t require anything special: the title is a widget, described by [build] just like the rest of the screen, and it updates its state automatically;
  • line 115: [ListView] is a column that scrolls when it exceeds the screen height. On a phone, this is almost always what’s needed: a [Column] that’s too tall would be cut off (and [Flutter] would display a yellow and black band, indicating an “overflow”);
  • lines 124–127: an input field ([TextField]): its controller, its label ([decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: ...)]), and [onChanged], the function called with each keystroke, along with the new text;
  • lines 130–135: the price. [keyboardType] selects the phone’s keyboard: in this case, the numeric keypad, including the comma. The entered text is converted to a number by [double.tryParse], which returns [null] if the text is not a number ([?? 0]: in this case, 0). The French comma is accepted by replacing it with a period;
  • lines 138–147: the quantity, with two buttons, “–” and “+.” [Row] places its children side by side; [Expanded] gives its child the entire remaining width. [IconButton]: a button that is just an icon. [onPressed: null] disables a button: the value cannot go below 0;
  • lines 152–159: the VAT rate, three “segmented” buttons, only one of which is selected. [selected] receives a set of values ([{_vatRate}]: a [Set] for an element), [onSelectionChanged] the new selected set;
  • lines 173–177: the results: three lines generated by the [_line] method;
  • line 190: one line of text per element in the history, generated by a [for] loop written in the list of children (see Example 03);
  • lines 202–208: a method that creates widgets. [{TextStyle? style}]: an optional named parameter that defaults to [null] if not provided. Breaking down a [build] into methods makes it more readable; Example 10 will show that it is often better to turn them into actual widgets.

We modify the price, quantity, and rate, then the item:

Each time the total incl. VAT changes, a line is added to the history. Changing the item resets the quantity to 1 (on the right).

The difference from [React] lies in one detail: [React] reflects the component’s behavior, which recreates its variables each time; the state must therefore be stored separately, via [useState]. In [Flutter], the state resides in an object ([State]), created once and retained: these are its fields, and [build] is just one of its methods. Therefore, we need neither hooks nor their rules (such as not calling them within a condition or managing their dependencies). The golden rule remains the same: we modify the state only in [setState], and [build] simply describes the screen based on the state.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 03: Writing a Widget Tree
docs.text:
There is no template language in [Flutter]: the screen is written in [Dart]. For conditions and loops, [Dart] provides tools for creating lists of children. This example displays a list of doctors, which can be filtered:

// =========================================================================
// lib/ex03_widgets/main.dart - writing a tree of widgets
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Flutter has no template language (no HTML, no JSX): the
// screens are written in Dart, with nested widget constructors.
// For conditions and loops, Dart offers tools made to
// build LISTS of children (children: [...]):
//   - if (condition) widget          : a child that only EXISTS if the
//                                      condition is true ("collection if");
//   - if (c) widgetA else widgetB    : one OR the other;
//   - condition ? widgetA : widgetB  : the same, in an expression;
//   - for (final x in list) widget   : one child per element of the list
//                                      ("collection for");
//   - ...otherList                   : the elements of another list,
//                                      inserted at this place ("spread");
//   - switch (value) { pattern => ... } : one value among several.
// And everything before the return of build() is ordinary code.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_svg/flutter_svg.dart';

// an "enumeration": the only possible values of a specialty
enum Specialty { generalPractitioner, pediatrician, cardiologist }

// a data class: its fields are final, a Doctor object never
// changes. The "const" constructor allows making constants of it
class Doctor {
  final int id;
  final String title;
  final String firstName;
  final String lastName;
  final Specialty specialty;
  final bool available;

  const Doctor(this.id, this.title, this.firstName, this.lastName, this.specialty, this.available);
}

const doctors = [
  Doctor(1, 'Mme', 'Marie', 'PELISSIER', Specialty.generalPractitioner, true),
  Doctor(2, 'Mr', 'Paul', 'TATOU', Specialty.pediatrician, false),
  Doctor(3, 'Melle', 'Sophie', 'DUPONT', Specialty.cardiologist, true),
];

// "one value among several, depending on a value": a switch EXPRESSION.
// The compiler checks that all the cases of the enumeration are handled
String label(Specialty s) => switch (s) {
  Specialty.generalPractitioner => 'general practitioner',
  Specialty.pediatrician => 'pediatrician',
  Specialty.cardiologist => 'cardiologist',
};

Icon icon(Specialty s) => switch (s) {
  Specialty.pediatrician => const Icon(Icons.child_care, color: Colors.orange),
  Specialty.cardiologist => const Icon(Icons.favorite, color: Colors.red),
  _ => const Icon(Icons.medical_services, color: Colors.teal), // "_": all the other cases
};

void main() {
  runApp(
    MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      home: const DoctorsPage(),
    ),
  );
}

class DoctorsPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const DoctorsPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<DoctorsPage> createState() => _DoctorsPageState();
}

class _DoctorsPageState extends State<DoctorsPage> {
  String _filter = ''; // the searched text
  bool _onlyAvailable = false;
  bool _showHelp = true;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // the displayed list: an ordinary variable, recomputed on each build()
    final text = _filter.trim().toLowerCase();
    final displayed = doctors
        .where(
          (m) =>
              (!_onlyAvailable || m.available) &&
              '${m.firstName} ${m.lastName} ${label(m.specialty)}'.toLowerCase().contains(text),
        )
        .toList();

    // "one of the three blocks": it is computed BEFORE the return, with ifs
    final Widget content;
    if (doctors.isEmpty) {
      content = const Text('No doctor.');
    } else if (displayed.isEmpty) {
      content = Text('No doctor matches "$_filter".', style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.deepOrange));
    } else {
      content = Column(
        children: [
          // one child per doctor: "collection for", with its rank (indexed)
          for (final (i, m) in displayed.indexed)
            // Opacity: the unavailable doctors are grayed out
            Opacity(
              opacity: m.available ? 1 : 0.5,
              // ListTile: a Material list row (icon, title, subtitle, trailing)
              child: ListTile(
                leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text('${i + 1}')),
                title: Text('${m.title} ${m.firstName} ${m.lastName}'),
                // Wrap: like a Row, but which wraps to the next line if space runs out
                subtitle: Wrap(
                  spacing: 6,
                  crossAxisAlignment: WrapCrossAlignment.center,
                  children: [icon(m.specialty), Text(label(m.specialty))],
                ),
                trailing: Chip(
                  label: Text(m.available ? 'available' : 'unavailable'),
                  // a color chosen by a conditional expression
                  backgroundColor: m.available ? Colors.green.shade100 : Colors.grey.shade300,
                ),
              ),
            ),
        ],
      );
    }

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        // an SVG image shipped with the application (assets/ folder, see pubspec.yaml)
        leading: Padding(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12), child: SvgPicture.asset('assets/doctor.svg')),
        title: const Text('Example 03 - the widgets'),
      ),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        children: [
          TextField(
            decoration: const InputDecoration(hintText: 'search...', prefixIcon: Icon(Icons.search)),
            onChanged: (value) => setState(() => _filter = value),
          ),
          // SwitchListTile: a switch, with its label
          SwitchListTile(
            title: const Text('available only'),
            value: _onlyAvailable,
            onChanged: (value) => setState(() => _onlyAvailable = value),
          ),
          Align(
            alignment: Alignment.centerLeft,
            child: TextButton(
              onPressed: () => setState(() => _showHelp = !_showHelp),
              child: Text(_showHelp ? 'Hide help' : 'Show help'),
            ),
          ),
          // "collection if": this widget only EXISTS if _showHelp is true
          if (_showHelp)
            Card(
              color: Colors.lightBlue.shade50,
              child: const Padding(
                padding: EdgeInsets.all(12),
                child: Text('Type a name or a specialty. The unavailable doctors are grayed out.'),
              ),
            ),
          content,
          const SizedBox(height: 12),
          // a COMPUTED style: the size of the text depends on the number of displayed doctors
          Text(
            '${displayed.length} doctor(s) displayed - the size of this text depends on it.',
            style: TextStyle(fontSize: 12 + displayed.length * 2.0),
          ),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • line 24: an enumeration: the only three possible values for a specialty ([Specialty.pediatrician]...);
  • lines 28–36: a data class. Its fields are [final]: a [Doctor] never changes. The constructor [Doctor(this.id, this.title, ...)] directly assigns its arguments to the fields of the same name. It is [const]: constant doctors can be created (line 39);
  • lines 47–50: “one value among several, depending on a value”: a [switch] expression (not an instruction), which has a value. Each case is written as [pattern => value]. For an enumeration, the compiler verifies that all cases are handled: adding a specialty without completing this [switch] would result in a compilation error;
  • lines 53–56: the same principle applies when selecting an icon; the pattern [_] means “all other cases.” The icons in [Material Design] are constants of the class [Icons];
  • lines 77–79: the screen state.

The method [build]:

  • lines 84–91: the displayed list: a variable recalculated with each call to [build]. [where] retains the elements that satisfy a condition; [toList()] converts the result into a list;
  • lines 94–100: one of three possible values, selected using [if] before [return]. A widget is a value like any other: it can be stored in a variable. [final Widget content;] declares the variable without initializing it: the compiler verifies that each branch assigns a value to it exactly once;
  • lines 103–117: the list. A `[for]` written to a literal list (`[children: [ ... ]]`) adds an element to it on each loop iteration: this is a “collection for.” [displayed.indexed] returns tuples (rank, doctor), which [(i, m)] “unpacks” into two variables;
  • line 106: [Opacity] makes its child partially transparent: unavailable doctors are grayed out. The value is calculated by the operator [? :];
  • lines 108–112: [ListTile] is the list entry for [Material Design]: a header element ([leading], here a disk showing the rank), a title, a subtitle, and an end element ([trailing]). All of these are widgets: any widgets. The subtitle is a [Wrap]: a [Row] that wraps to the next line when there isn’t enough space (on a phone, the icon and specialty wouldn’t always fit next to the “available” label);
  • Lines 117–120: a “bullet” ([Chip]), whose text and color depend on the doctor. [Colors.green.shade100]: a light shade of green.

[return]:

  • line 131: an image SVG, included with the application (folder [assets/], declared in [pubspec.yaml]). [Flutter] cannot render SVG on its own: the [flutter_svg] package provides the [SvgPicture] widget. For an image PNG or JPEG, [Flutter] has the widget [Image.asset];
  • Lines 138–139: the search field. [hintText] is the grayed-out text displayed as long as the field is empty; [prefixIcon] is an icon on the left. This time, no controller: we only need the entered value, received by [onChanged];
  • lines 142–145: a toggle switch, with its label: a list item that you tap to toggle;
  • line 150: an anonymous function, written directly within the parameter: it toggles the state;
  • lines 155–160: an “if collection”: the help card exists only if [_showHelp] is true. There is no “hidden” widget: when the condition is false, the list of children has one fewer item;
  • line 163: the content selected earlier;
  • lines 167–168: a computed style: the text size depends on the number of doctors displayed.

To summarize the tools in [Dart] that replace, within a list of children, what other frameworks write in their templates:

In DartRoleif (condition) widgeta child that exists only if the condition is trueif (c) widgetA else widgetBone or the othercondition? widgetA : widgetBeither one, in an expressionfor (final x in list) widgetone child per element in the list...otherListthe elements of another list, inserted at this location...[widgetA, widgetB]multiple children at once (often after an `if` statement)switch (value) { pattern => widget }one child among several, based on a value

At startup, then after typing “gen” and hiding the help, then with “xyz”:

docs.title: 3.4. Example 04: Events
docs.text:
An interactive widget receives functions as parameters to be called when something happens; these are often called “callbacks.” This example manages a to-do list:

// =========================================================================
// lib/ex04_events/main.dart - reacting to the user's actions
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// An interactive widget receives as parameters the FUNCTIONS to call when
// something happens ("callbacks"):
//   - onPressed: f                  : f is called on a press (buttons);
//   - onPressed: () => remove(t)    : an anonymous function, to pass its
//                                     own arguments;
//   - onChanged, onSubmitted...     : the function receives a piece of data (the
//                                     text, the checked box...);
//   - GestureDetector               : adds gestures (tap, long press,
//                                     double tap, drag...) to
//                                     ANY widget;
//   - Dismissible                   : swiping a row to remove it,
//                                     the typical gesture of a mobile.
// To act on an input field from the code (read or clear its
// text, give it the focus), we attach a CONTROLLER and a FocusNode to it.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter/services.dart';

class Task {
  final int id;
  final String label;
  bool done;

  Task(this.id, this.label, {this.done = false});
}

void main() {
  runApp(
    MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      theme: ThemeData(colorSchemeSeed: Colors.indigo),
      home: const TasksPage(),
    ),
  );
}

class TasksPage extends StatefulWidget {
  const TasksPage({super.key});

  @override
  State<TasksPage> createState() => _TasksPageState();
}

class _TasksPageState extends State<TasksPage> {
  final List<Task> _tasks = [
    Task(1, 'Install Flutter', done: true),
    Task(2, 'Read the chapter on events'),
  ];
  final List<String> _log = [];
  // the controller of the field: its text (reading, writing);
  // the FocusNode: its focus (the cursor and the keyboard of the phone)
  final _field = TextEditingController();
  final _focus = FocusNode();
  // a field of the State object that is NOT displayed: modifying it
  // requires no setState
  int _nextId = 3;

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _field.dispose();
    _focus.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  void _trace(String message) {
    final t = TimeOfDay.now();
    _log.insert(0, '${t.format(context)} $message');
  }

  // called by the button AND by the Enter key of the keyboard (onSubmitted)
  void _add() {
    final label = _field.text.trim();
    if (label.isEmpty) {
      return;
    }
    setState(() {
      _tasks.add(Task(_nextId++, label));
      _trace('added "$label"');
    });
    _field.clear();
    // the focus returns to the field: the next task can be typed
    _focus.requestFocus();
  }

  void _toggle(Task task, bool done) {
    setState(() {
      task.done = done;
      _trace('"${task.label}": ${done ? 'done' : 'to do'}');
    });
  }

  void _remove(Task task, String how) {
    setState(() {
      _tasks.remove(task);
      _trace('removed "${task.label}" ($how)');
    });
  }

  // the details of a tap: its position, relative to the touched widget
  void _position(TapDownDetails details) {
    final p = details.localPosition;
    setState(() => _trace('tap at (${p.dx.round()}, ${p.dy.round()})'));
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('Example 04 - the events')),
      body: ListView(
        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
        children: [
          Row(
            children: [
              Expanded(
                // CallbackShortcuts: keyboard shortcuts (a physical
                // keyboard: computer, emulator, tablet); Esc clears the field
                child: CallbackShortcuts(
                  bindings: {const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.escape): _field.clear},
                  child: TextField(
                    controller: _field,
                    focusNode: _focus,
                    decoration: const InputDecoration(hintText: 'new task (Esc to clear)'),
                    // the "Enter" key of the phone's keyboard
                    textInputAction: TextInputAction.done,
                    onSubmitted: (_) => _add(),
                  ),
                ),
              ),
              const SizedBox(width: 8),
              FilledButton(onPressed: _add, child: const Text('Add')),
            ],
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 12),
          for (final t in _tasks)
            // Dismissible: swiping the row to the left removes it.
            // key: the IDENTITY of the row, so that Flutter knows which one
            // has disappeared (see the explanation in the course)
            Dismissible(
              key: ValueKey(t.id),
              direction: DismissDirection.endToStart,
              background: Container(
                color: Colors.red.shade100,
                alignment: Alignment.centerRight,
                padding: const EdgeInsets.only(right: 16),
                child: const Icon(Icons.delete),
              ),
              onDismissed: (_) => _remove(t, 'swipe'),
              child: CheckboxListTile(
                // the box is ON THE LEFT, as in a task list
                controlAffinity: ListTileControlAffinity.leading,
                value: t.done,
                // the box passes its new value (bool?, hence the "!")
                onChanged: (checked) => _toggle(t, checked!),
                title: Text(
                  t.label,
                  style: t.done ? const TextStyle(decoration: TextDecoration.lineThrough, color: Colors.grey) : null,
                ),
                // an anonymous function: the task of THIS row as argument
                secondary: IconButton(
                  icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline, color: Colors.red),
                  onPressed: () => _remove(t, 'button'),
                ),
              ),
            ),
          const SizedBox(height: 12),
          // GestureDetector: any widget becomes sensitive to gestures
          GestureDetector(
            onTapDown: _position,
            onDoubleTap: () => setState(() => _trace('double tap')),
            onLongPress: () => setState(() => _trace('long press')),
            child: Container(
              height: 80,
              alignment: Alignment.center,
              decoration: BoxDecoration(color: const Color(0xFFE7F5FF), borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8)),
              child: const Text('Touch this area (tap, double tap, long press)'),
            ),
          ),
          const SizedBox(height: 16),
          Text('Log', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleSmall),
          for (final line in _log) Text(line, style: const TextStyle(fontSize: 12)),
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
  • lines 23–28: a task. [done] is not [final]: we’ll modify it. [{this.done = false}]: an optional named parameter, with its default value;
  • lines 49–53: the state: the list of tasks and an event log;
  • lines 56–57: to manipulate the input field from within the code, two objects are associated with it: a controller ([TextEditingController]), which provides access to its text, and a [FocusNode], which provides access to its focus (the blinking cursor and the phone’s keyboard, which opens when a field has focus);
  • Line 60: A field of the [State] object that is not displayed: modifying it does not require a [setState]. This is what [React] calls a “reference” ([useRef]); in [Flutter], it is an ordinary field;
  • lines 63–66: the controller and the [FocusNode] are released when the screen disappears;
  • lines 69–71: one additional line at the top of the log. [TimeOfDay] is the time of day from [Flutter]; [format(context)] formats it according to the conventions of the application’s language;
  • lines 75–86: adding a task, triggered by the button AND by the Enter key on the keyboard. We read the text in the control ([_field.text]), add the task (in [setState]), clear the field ([_field.clear()]), and return focus to it ([_focus.requestFocus()]): you can now type the next task;
  • Lines 89–92: Check or uncheck a task: We modify the [Task] object itself, in [setState]. Unlike [React], there is no need to create a new list: [setState] notifies [Flutter] that the status has changed, regardless of how it changed;
  • lines 96–99: deletion, either via the button or by swiping (see below);
  • Lines 104–106: The function called when the bottom area is tapped. It receives the event details: in this case, [localPosition], the finger's position relative to the tapped widget.

The [build] method:

  • Lines 121–122: [CallbackShortcuts] associates keyboard shortcuts with functions for a physical keyboard (computer, emulator, tablet with keyboard): the Esc key clears the field. [{ key: function }] is a literal [Map];
  • Lines 124–129: The input field, linked to its controller and its [FocusNode]. [textInputAction] selects the “Enter” key on the phone’s keyboard; [onSubmitted] is called when it is pressed, along with the text (which is not used: the parameter is named [_], by convention);
  • line 134: the button calls the same method;
  • lines 138–151: one line per task, in a [Dismissible]: a widget that you swipe with your finger to remove, the typical gesture for a list on a phone. [direction]: only to the left; [background]: what appears below the row during the swipe (a trash can icon on a red background); [onDismissed]: the function called when the row is swiped off the screen;
  • line 143: the key for [Dismissible]. When a list of widgets changes, [Flutter] compares the old list to the new one to determine which widgets to keep: without a key, it pairs them by their rank (the first to the first, the second to the second, and so on). If the first task disappears, the second would take its place… with the state of the first. A key gives each widget an identity: [Flutter] then matches the widgets by their keys. The key must be unique among siblings and stable: the task’s identifier, not its rank. A [Dismissible] requires a key;
